speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before the committee begins to consider the income tax resolution in detail I think it might be helpful if I were to give an outline of the proposals before us. It may be helpful if I do so in some detail in order to provide members of the committee with a general understanding of what is involved. I shall, of course, be glad to go into more extended detail on any particular item when the time comes. However, as much of this resolution is highly technical, a broad, general description at the beginning may be helpful.
Although there is only one income tax resolution, it is divided into 16 paragraphs, and it has been customary in the past for the committee to consider each paragraph in turn. Of the 16 paragraphs, nine propose relieving amendments, one is partly relieving, four propose legislation to correct the law where it has been found to have unintended results, and two paragraphs might be described as consequential since they relate to the proposed extension of the payment of family allowances.
Under the proposed new arrangement with the provinces announced by the Prime Minister on April 20, the room made available for the provinces to impose their own income tax on individuals without increasing the total tax load from that source will be increased for the 1965 and the 1966 taxation years. Provision for this should be made in this year's amendments to the Income Tax Act. Therefore when the committee reaches the end of paragraph 16 I shall propose an amendment to add a paragraph 17 to the resolution to increase the relevant deduction 20220-166
Income Tax Act
from federal individual income tax otherwise payable, from 19 per cent to 21 per cent for 1965, and from 20 per cent to 24 per cent for 1966. The bill to be introduced after this resolution has been considered by the committee will, as usual, contain a number of additional amendments most of which will be of a technical or drafting nature.
I should perhaps mention one relieving amendment of some general interest which is planned for the bill but which is not described in the resolution. This is an amendment to provide that payments made by the Federal Republic of Germany as compensation to victims of nazi persecution who are now living in Canada shall be exempt from Canadian income tax. The payments referred to are those which are also exempt from tax by Germany. The details of this exemption will be provided when the bill is introduced.
The first paragraph of the resolution proposes that the deduction in computing income now allowed for tuition fees paid by full time students be extended to allow part time students to deduct tuition fees paid to an educational institution in Canada. A large number of people in Canada take classes at night to obtain a matriculation certificate or a university degree. Many of the teachers in our schools take courses during the summer vacation period to improve their teaching qualifications. A large number of our young people take courses in business colleges or in vocational training schools to equip themselves for employment. Tuition fees must be paid for this instruction, but these courses are not usually of sufficient duration to qualify the participant as a full time student. It is hoped that the proposed change to allow a deduction for tuition fees paid by part time students will encourage and help more Canadians to acquire the training and skills which are more and more demanded in our increasingly complex economy.
The second paragraph of the resolution is also related to the pursuit of education. It proposes that a taxpayer be allowed to claim his brother or sister as a dependant for income tax purposes, even when the brother or sister is 21 years of age or over, if he or she is in full time attendance at school or university. At present a taxpayer may claim his adult brother or sister as a dependant only if he or she is dependent by reason of mental or physical infirmity.
The third, fourth and fifth paragraphs of the resolution deal with the program of tax incentives for new manufacturing or processing businesses in designated areas of slower growth. The act now provides an exemption from income tax for the income earned by a new manufacturing or processing business in

Income Tax Act
a designated area during the first 36 months after it commences commercial operations. At present such businesses have to commence commercial operations within the 24 month period that started on December 5, 1963. It is proposed to amend the act to extend this period so that it will run from December 5, 1963 to March 31, 1967. This extension will give larger developments in designated areas a more reasonable chance to complete their capital construction programs and to commence commercial operations within the time limit. I may say to hon. members of the committee that I was impressed with representations made to the effect that the previous time limit of 24 months was too short. With the proposed change the government is very hopeful that these incentives will result in some important developments being undertaken in designated areas; that is, in places where they can do the most good in providing needed jobs.
It was also announced in the budget speech that the privilege of writing off new manufacturing machinery acquired for use by a new manufacturing or processing business in a designated area at the accelerated rate of 50 per cent will be continued with respect to machinery acquired up until April 1, 1967. The accelerated rate of 20 per cent for writing off new buildings will also continue to apply to new buildings acquired in designated areas until April 1, 1967. This extension of the capital cost allowance provisions will be made by changes in the income tax regulations and does not require amendments to the act.
On the subject of capital cost allowance regulations, it will be recalled that the budget speech also announced an increase in the rate of allowance for heavy mobile machinery used to excavate or move earth or rock for use in compacting road building materials. The amendment to the income tax regulations to increase the rate of capital cost allowance on such machinery from 30 per cent to 50 per cent has now been passed. The change in the legislation concerning designated areas, proposed by paragraph 4 of the resolution, is a technical amendment to the rules for determining if a new business is being carried on in a designated area.
The change proposed by paragraph 5 is intended to deal with the situation which would arise if an area which is now a designated area should cease to become designated because it no longer needs the benefit of special tax concessions. The proposed amendment will provide that where a taxpayer has commenced, or made plans to commence, a new manufacturing or processing business in an area during the time when it was designated, that area shall be deemed

to continue to be a designated area for purposes of the application of the act to that particular business. The purpose of this amendment is to make sure that taxpayers who have taken steps to avail themselves of the tax benefits offered in designated areas shall not lose any of those benefits if an area should cease to be designated.
In paragraph 6 a change is proposed concerning scientific research. It is proposed that the act be amended to make it clear that expenditures of a current nature for scientific research carried on outside Canada shall be deductible if the research is related to the taxpayer's business. This amendment is intended to restore a deduction which existed before 1962, but which was removed by a change in the wording of the law in that year. For many years companies in Canada have made payments to their parent companies abroad, or to other non-residents, for the right to share in the results of research and development programs carried on outside Canada. These long-standing arrangements under which Canadian companies have obtained the results of research carried on abroad have provided Canadian industry with valuable processes, techniques and knowhow, and denial of the right to deduct payments for this information would restrict this flow of information with detrimental results for the Canadian economy. The proposed amendment will not change the incentive provided in the act for increased research in Canada. Taxpayers will continue to be allowed to deduct 150 per cent of the amount by which their research expenditures in Canada exceed their expenditures in a base period.
Paragraph 7 proposes legislation to allow a taxpayer to deduct amounts spent by him in connection with preparing a notice of objection to a tax assessment or in appealing a tax assessment to the tax appeal board or a court.
Paragraphs 8, 9 and 10 propose changes concerning registered pension plans. The first of these is a somewhat technical amendment to the rules concerning the deduction of amounts contributed into registered pension plans. The purpose of this amendment is to cover situations where members of a pension plan who were contributors under the plan for some past years, and were not contributors in some other past years, now want to make lump sum or annual contributions into the plan in respect of those past years.
Under the amendment proposed in paragraph 9 an employer will have 120 days instead of the present 60 days after the end of his taxation year to make his payment to a pension plan for his employees. This is

intended to give employers who base part of their contributions upon yearly profits a longer time in which to ascertain those profits. The amendment to pension plan legislation proposed under paragraph 10 is to close a possible loophole. It has been made necessary because it was held in a recent court decision that a refund of contributions from a pension plan to an employer did not constitute income in his hands.
Paragraph 11 will not be of wide general interest because it refers to a special situation which sometimes arises between a taxpayer and another person with whom he is not dealing at arm's length. A new set of rules is proposed to deal with the case where such a taxpayer, who keeps his accounts on an accrual basis, owes an amount, such as interest, but has not actually paid this amount in the year he deducts it for income tax purposes. The amendment will prevent unintended advantages being received by some taxpayers but it will also be relieving in certain other cases.
The amendment proposed by paragraph 12 will result in the rate of non-resident withholding tax on certain dividends paid after December 31, 1964, remaining at 15 per cent. Other changes which are consequential upon retaining the 15 per cent rate of tax on dividends paid by a corporation that does not have a degree of Canadian ownership are also proposed.
In paragraph 13 an amendment is proposed to make clear that where a partner sells his interest in a partnership and this interest includes depreciable property the appropriate part of the amount he receives as selling price shall be deemed to be received on account of the disposal of the depreciable property. This amendment will make it possible to apply to usual rules related to capital cost allowances in such circumstances.
Paragraphs 14 and 15 are consequential upon the plan to continue family allowances to children who are 16 and 17 years of age and who are continuing their education. The Income Tax Act provides that the amount of $300 is deductible for dependant children qualified for family allowances and $550 for dependants not qualified for family allowances. The budget speech announced the government's plan to amend the Family Allowances Act so that children aged 16 and 17 may be registered to receive family allowances starting in 1964; but since it will take some time to introduce this legislation and establish the administrative machinery the allowances are not likely to be available before the end of the summer. Since only three or four payments are likely to be available in 1964 it is not planned to make the full reduction from $550 to $300 in the 20220-1661
Income Tax Act
amount that may be deducted for children aged 16 or 17 in respect of whom family allowances are paid in 1964. The reduction proposed is only about one third of the difference between $550 and $300, or $80. This leaves a deduction of $470 for dependent children aged 16 or 17 in respect of whom new allowances are received in 1964.
For 1965 and subsequent years the definition of a child qualified for family allowance is to be amended to include a child who is 16 or 17 years of age at the end of the year if an allowance under the Family Allowances Act is paid in respect of the child in the year for any month after the month in which the child becomes 16 years of age.
Paragraph 16, which is long and complicated, is designed to tighten section 139A of the act which defines when a corporation has a degree of Canadian ownership. As usually happens with legislation that breaks new ground, loopholes were discovered in the definition contained in the amendments that were passed last fall. A great deal of time and effort has gone into the drafting of the revised definition with the object of plugging the existing loopholes and making it quite clear that the incentives offered will be available only to those foreign-controlled companies that make equity shares available to Canadians.
Since March 16 when the resolution was made public I have had conversations with a number of tax practitioners, both accountants and lawyers, who have made a number of helpful suggestions for further changes of a minor character. These will be incorporated in the bill.
I have already mentioned that a paragraph 17 will be proposed, when we reach that point, to provide increased abatements of the federal income tax on individuals in accordance with the recently announced arrangements with the provinces.
All of these proposed amendments are recommended to the committee to assist education, to extend incentives for the development of designated areas, to carry out announced policies and to improve the provisions of the act. I shall be glad to explain each paragraph in more detail as the committee considers each in turn.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the minister, in which he reviewed very briefly the individual sections comprising the group which we have before us. I am not sure what should be our procedure. I remember a year ago we were held strictly to dealing with each resolution in turn. Frankly, that is all I propose to do in discussing any of them this afternoon,

Income Tax Act
but I presume that it is open to us to wander somewhat over the whole field because of the fact that some of them are interrelated, as the minister stated. Some of them deal with education, others with various facets which are actually quite closely connected, and I think it would enable full discussion in committee and would probably shorten the proceedings if we were to refer to more than one at any one time. As far as I am concerned, at the moment I intend only to deal with the first section which is before us.
I wonder if I might make a suggestion to the minister. The minister has said-as a matter of fact, he mentioned it to me casually on Friday evening-that he is proposing to bring in an amendment to one of the existing sections dealing with abatement. I quite realize he does not want to move it at this time but when we come to the proposed paragraph 17 I think it will facilitate discussion to have had the amendment placed before us now, so that we can give consideration to it in the interim rather than having to deal with it for the first time when we come to the last paragraph, and perhaps having to hold up the passage of the resolution until we have had a chance to consider the amendment. I suggest to the minister that perhaps he should do that.
As the minister has said, the first paragraph deals with assistance to education, and I am quite sure the committee will welcome any move in this direction. This broadens the policy which was introduced into the Income Tax Act in 1961, I think, by which we provided for the deduction of tuition fees of university students. This provision goes further and covers the four classes 'set out in the four subsections here, all of which I think are highly desirable.
As the minister said, these deductions will be particularly beneficial to part time students, to students taking courses in the now greatly enlarged technical and vocational training schools which have been established and are growing so rapidly, to students who are attending night school and to students who are attending summer school. I was interested in reading in one of the Toronto papers, after the minister brought forward the resolution, the fact that in the schools of Toronto, a city in which the minister has more than an academic interest I presume, there were 4,700 students taking part time courses in the wintertime and 7,700 students taking summer school courses at the University of Toronto and York University, I assume. This is a very substantial number and they will receive some measure of assistance through the proposal now before us.

There are so many facets of the educational problem which one could discuss, but this is not the time to discuss them in detail. However, I have noticed statements issued by some of the school and university authorities in Toronto referring to summer training and the assistance given to teachers and college graduates in better preparing themselves for the teaching profession. This is certainly something that is highly desirable. All of these things are good. We have been told about extended family allowances. There has been talk about a student loan fund. This matter is not before us now but I presume it will be at some future date. There are various procedures suggested for the assistance of education and the assistance of students, and this is all to the good in so far as the individual is concerned.
But the problem goes much deeper than that, of course. We not only have to provide assistance to students who wish to go to university or other schools. The problem, of course is more acute in the case of universities. We also have to provide teachers and accommodation for the students and teachers. In looking at a national magazine over the week end I was intrigued to read that at one university in the United States, not one of the largest by a long shot, there were 5,900 applications for entrance into university in the past year and the university was only able to accept 1,100 out of 5,900 applications. This shows something of the pressure on universities and schools not only in the United States but also in Canada.
As I said, the time to discuss these matters is not on this particular resolution, but when the minister's estimates are before the house later this session and we are dealing with university grants and methods of assistance to universities I give the minister fair notice that I hope he will be prepared to discuss these matters at some length. I think this is one of the most pressing problems with which the minister and the nation are confronted, and as much as we approve of the individual items of assistance which are before us, they are really only scratching the surface-except for their help to individuals-of the problem in the nation as a whole and a great deal more attention has to be given to the educational problem in the immediate future.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure I speak for the whole committee, no one could help but agree that the steps proposed in paragraph 1 are helpful and desirable and ones which I think will commend themselves to the favourable consideration of the committee. I notice that the deduction for tuition fees only applies if the amount is over $25. If the amount is $26 does that mean that the

student will be able to deduct the full $26 or only the excess over $25? Although it is not exactly relevant to this paragraph it is relevant to the problem of assistance to students, and I wonder whether the minister could tell the committee now when he proposes to deal with the matter of university student loans, a measure which was mentioned in the speech from the throne and has been forecast by the Prime Minister and the minister himself. Perhaps he could advise us of that when he is dealing with this paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would be glad to answer those two questions now if that is agreeable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. To give effect to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and in view of the fact that the minister has referred to a proposed amendment, and considering also that the amendment can only refer to the resolution itself rather than to a specific paragraph, perhaps it might be a good idea to have the proposed amendment moved now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move the following amendment:
That the Income Tax Act resolution be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
"17. That the income tax otherwise payable by an individual in respect of income earned in a province of Canada be reduced by
(a)	21 per cent for the 1965 taxation year, rather than 19 per cent, and
(b)	24 per cent for the 1966 taxation year, rather than 20 per cent."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to the two specific questions, Mr. Chairman, may I say there is always a problem, I suppose, in working out any amendments to the Income Tax Act as to how far you go for complete equity and precision and what you do about an excess of complexity in the administration of the law. It is proposed that any fees of $25 or less be disallowed and any fees of $26 or over be allowed in full. I quite agree that this is not perfection, but I am sure that if we reach that perfection we will arrive at a tax law that the ordinary person cannot understand. One of my colleagues said today -I hope I will not be pressed to divulge the name-that the preparation of his income tax return was beyond him and he called upon me for help as an ex-practitioner in this field. However, I was never able to make out my own so I cannot help other people.
It is a simpler form this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, with every amendment the forms become less simple. The other question my hon. friend asked was when the legislation would be introduced respecting
Income Tax Act
student loans. This will be introduced separately and obviously will not be a part of these proposed amendments. We are working on that legislation. I cannot promise a particular date, but I certainly think they should be introduced as early as possible.

I certainly am in agreement with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in his expression of satisfaction with regard to these student allowances. However, they do seem to me to be rather meagre. There is one point on which I had hoped the minister might have some new ideas and that is with regard to the provision of an allowance for textbooks. They constitute a very heavy burden on students in the course of their education. While the deduction on account of fees is certainly to be commended, it would seem to me it should include all the costs of their educational courses.
I find it difficult to understand why the minister should confine this sort of allowance to students, when there are other sections of the community that suffer from the same sort of disability for which they get no compensation at all. I have in mind, for instance, the heavy expenses some groups of workers have to incur in order to earn their livelihood. I have in mind particularly those engaged in the logging industry in my own constituency, where they have to buy extremely expensive clothing and footwear for which they get no allowance whatever in connection with income tax. This seems to me to be a legitimate expense incurred by the necessity of the way they earn their livelihood. I should like to see some idea of that type going all through the income tax provisions.
In so far as the allowance for students is concerned, I was disturbed not long ago to note a comment in the newspapers, whether correct or not I do not know, from the premier of Quebec to the effect that these allowances were an invasion of provincial rights. I have no means of knowing whether or not the federal government is taking any note of this view, but I would suggest to the government this provision is an arrangement being made between the government of Canada and Canadian citizens wherever they may live. It is no business of any provincial government. I hope the government will not accept the position taken by the premier of Quebec because I think it would be another dangerous step toward the disintegration of our central, national authority.
I should like to turn for a few moments, Mr. Chairman, to some of the other paragraphs, in the resolution, namely paragraph 4.

Income Tax Act
I should like the minister to give some explanation of the method that will be used to determine effectively when a new business started.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman; perhaps you could clarify now whether this is the procedure we are going to follow or whether we are going to take the resolution paragraph by paragraph?
It was my understanding the whole of the resolution was before us, but I am subject to correction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is correct. At the moment, the whole resolution is before the committee and if later, in the course of discussion, there were unanimous consent to study the resolution paragraph by paragraph, we could do it. At the moment, we are considering the whole resolution.

This was my understanding, Mr. Chairman. I wonder if the minister could explain to us later just how he is going to distinguish between a genuine new enterprise starting in a designated area and a wholly owned subsidiary of a well established company which is starting business in this area?
I should like some elaboration of section 5 with regard to the provisions for particular companies making application for tax exemption in federally designated areas, and being in a position to take advantage of the tax exemption at a later date after the designation has been removed. I should like to know, in the first place, how long a period is to be allowed for such an application before a person commences operation in the designated area? If he is permitted to wait perhaps for several years until there is a proper economic climate in that area to determine whether it is going to be profitable for him to start a particular business, it seems to me we are defeating the intention of this amendment, in that companies may very well take advantage of this provision unless there is some rather clearly defined limit. There may be some time elapse before they start a new enterprise.
In so far as section 6 is concerned, I am sure most people will welcome this encouragement to research in Canada. Again, I have a question to raise. What is the particular definition of research that is to be used? Is it to be basic research or is a company to be permitted to have a deduction for what would be classed as technical or specific research designed to produce some development that later may be patented, thereby reserving to this particular company all the benefits of

this research for which it had received this tax exemption. It would seem to be most important that we should know that. I would suspect a large part of industrial research that is undertaken would fall into the category of development or process that could later be patented, and the returns from it be channelled into the coffers of one company. I believe the purpose of such an amendment would be to encourage research from which the whole community could benefit.
Under section 12, Mr. Chairman, it would be interesting to know exactly what was the cause of the reduction from 20 per cent to 15 per cent? What was the purpose that was sought to be served by that action? Perhaps later on the minister will be able to enlighten us.
In the following sections we have a provision to the effect that where a taxpayer has disposed of his interest in a partnership, such part of the consideration as is reasonable in the circumstances shall be deemed to be proceeds of disposition-I am always a little bit uneasy when I see such terms as "reasonable" or "adequate" in legislation. I wonder if the minister would be able to tell us what yardstick, what consideration, is to be used to determine whether or not such a proportion is reasonable? These are some of the questions that should arise now, Mr. Chairman. While one could discuss the whole basis of our income tax policies under this resolution, I do not propose to do so today, except to put in again a little plug for the consideration of a capital gains tax in Canada. Beyond that, Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to wait until we discuss the items in greater detail under the minister's estimates.

I agree, Mr. Chairman, with the suggestion of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, that while the whole resolution is before us it would probably expedite our discussion if we took it one paragraph at a time. For that reason, I only want to spend three or four minutes to draw to the minister's attention one or two things about which he may wish to move amendments when we come to the particular paragraph concerned.
So far as paragraph 1 is concerned, I just wish to say we add our support to this matter of being able to deduct the cost of tuition fees from income tax. It is something that is justified, but we believe it is only a step in the right direction because there are still some very serious injustices concerning things that are actually deductible from taxable income. This is particularly true when applied to people who have spent a lot of time to acquire an education, which becomes the tool by which they earn their income. So far as

postgraduate studies are concerned, we think there would be every justification for including as deductions from taxable income some of the other expenses involved when a person must go away from home, in addition to the actual amount paid for tuition fees.
I am not clear what will happen under paragraphs 14 and 15 in the event that Premier Lesage manages to make arrangements with the federal government to take a cash consideration instead of having these family allowances paid direct by the federal government to children aged 16 and 17 years in the province of Quebec. We do not know whether Premier Lesage is going to refuse these payments. We know there have been some negotiations between the federal government and the Quebec provincial government, and it would be reasonably safe to say these negotiations covered the matter of family allowances.
If these discussions culminate in an agreement whereby there is a payment to the Quebec provincial government, in lieu of making these payments direct to the children, then it would be necessary to have another amendment to the Income Tax Act to equate the final results of this kind of arrangement for the people in the other provinces. I am sure the minister would agree it would be an injustice if a deduction of $550 were allowed for children age 16 and 17 years in the province of Quebec and only $300 for children in the same age group in the other provinces of Canada, while at the same time there was a payment out of the federal treasury to the Quebec provincial government matching the aggregate amount of these allowances.
Perhaps the minister intends to move an appropriate amendment, or it may be a stage has not been reached in the negotiations so that an announcement can be made regarding the final arrangements. Other than that, we are willing to follow the course outlined by the speakers on behalf of the two other parties, to take each paragraph in turn and confine our remarks to it.

Mr. Chairman, when I rise to discuss taxes, I am always reminded of that story of the seven year old boy who got lost in the Quebec income tax offices and the tax inspectors, looking for that child's mother, were shouting all over the place: whose $300 deduction is this? That is to show you a little Mr. Chairman, the turn of mind of those tax inspectors, of those people who only think in terms of an act, in terms of the greatest zeal they can display.
Income Tax Act
Last year, when the same budget resolutions came before us, I remember very clearly mentioning to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) that the drafters of that legislation-in the first place, let us consider it, if you will, from the literary point of view-that the drafting of that legislation especially the one coming from the Department of Finance, was complicated and exceedingly long, and most of the time incomprehensible, even for those who are responsible for the administration of the Income Tax Act. They just cannot make it out, so we can expect they will administer it somewhat at random.
For instance, if we take paragraph 16, we have a whole page, commencing on page 6 and ending on page 7, a whole page where there is not even one period. In short, there is only one sentence covering a whole page.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest it is almost a world record to be able to write a one-page sentence. When we start reading it, we come across right and left incidentals and once we have read it-imagine-we wonder how that amendment to the act can be fully understood by the officials of the various income tax offices all across the country.
The act itself is complicated in its wording, its subject matter, its sources of reference and its numbering.
Is it any wonder then that it is misinterpreted in various income tax offices throughout Canada? Is it any wonder also that it brings about unfair treatment for taxpayers and that they often have good cause to complain about income tax inspectors or assessors?
There is one office in particular about which I would like to talk this afternoon. It is located in the Quebec district. I am singling it out because it is probably the one with which I deal most often, since I get a great number of complaints about it.
My constituency comes within the purview of the Quebec income tax office. In that office discriminatory and arbitrary decisions are taken, dictatorial decisions are taken without any inquiries or examination of any kind, and when the taxpayer is not satisfied, he is told: Put in a complaint, put in an appeal, or come and see us in Quebec city.
The Quebec district office is 135 miles away from my constituency, so you can well imagine how difficult it is for an ordinary worker who earns his living by the day, to go to the Quebec city office during business hours.
I would like to mention one of those cases to illustrate how this act we are voting today can be outrageously applied in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I fear the hon. gentleman is moving away from the

Income Tax Act
resolution before the committee. I think he is discussing the administration of the Income Tax Act rather than the terms of the resolution now before us. I would prefer it if he would remain with the resolution that is before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, on this point of order, we are now on an income tax resolution, and it was stated before Your Honour took the chair that the resolution was in a general way before the committee. Its wording starts:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other thingscertain specific things. It is the whole gist of the resolution and of the amendment of the Income Tax Act that is before the committee, and I would therefore submit it is strictly pertinent to the discussion to mention the way the act is administered; and that is what the hon. member for Lapointe is doing. I would respectfully submit he is within the rules in bringing up these matters.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, I should like to point out that I only made preliminary remarks on the wording of the act, on the manner in which it is written, on the manner in which it is divided into paragraphs, and in regard to its phraseology. It is to illustrate how badly this text is worded that I speak of the doings of the income tax inspectors which are ridiculous and arbitrary, because the very act we wish to pass is badly written. For example I can quote a sentence, that is section 16, which I would challenge you to read and tell me, within an hour, its exact meaning.
You will realize, then, that tax inspectors are unable to understand-that is the point I wish to make-and why it is that their interpretation is wrong. It is precisely because the legislation is poorly written. This is, in addition to the arguments put forth by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), another point I want to make before we approve such poorly written legislation and I want to show you the disastrous effects of this poorly written text which does not make sense.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I must agree with the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue that since the resolution before us deals with amendments to the Income Tax Act the hon. member who has the floor has a right to make some suggestions about the administration of the act, both as it stands and also, perhaps, in anticipation of certain problems which he thinks
[The Deputy Chairman.]
are likely to arise with respect to the administration of some of these amendments which are before us, now-and, of course, the whole of the resolution is before us, not just parts of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I should like to point out to hon. members on this point of order that we have a resolution before us from the Department of Finance and that the administration of the Income Tax Act is a responsibility of the Department of National Revenue. While hon. members are free to make any comments they wish regarding the Income Tax Act, these will only be in order provided they are related to the resolution before us. I have no intention in the world of restricting debate but I think it would be wise if, in our remarks, we were to relate those observations to the resolution which is now before us even though they might concern the administration of the act.

Mr. Chairman, I shall right away relate remarks to the resolution before us by saying that the doings of the officials of the tax department depend on the way this text is drafted, which makes it hard to understand.
For instance, I have here a rather incomprehensible case namely the case of charity receipts. In the case I have here, the department wrote to the taxpayer after his tax return had been accepted: Your charity receipts have been cut by such an amount. No investigation was made, despite the fact that the legislation we want to pass provides that if the person supplied charity receipts-that is written into the act-the amount can be deducted from the tax, provided the total receipts do not exceed 10 per cent of the salary. But inspectors do not understand that or they want to make a show of zeal to get a promotion, and that to the prejudice of taxpayers.
Inspectors write to the taxpayer and say: After investigation, we have decided to cut from $400 to $300 the amount you claim as charitable donations. The taxpayer wonders why and says: Well, I supplied the charity receipts, I am entitled to that under the act and you refuse it to me. The inspector replies: An investigation was made and we are not going to change our minds.
That is where the taxpayer writes to us and puts the matter in our hands. I have a briefcase full of problems like that, but I should like to state only a few.
Then we write to the Quebec income tax office and ask: Why did you cut down the allowance for charitable donations of this taxpayer? The taxation division replies a

little more intelligently and decently, saying: After inquiry, it has been deemed advisable to cut the allowance for charitable donations; however, if the taxpayer can account for his receipts, they will be accepted. But the taxpayer has already accounted for his receipts, since they were duly signed, in most cases by the parish priest, who is an honourable and respected person. They are signed by the parish priest who is told to warrant them. Then the parish priest has to write to the taxation division officials and tell them: I am surprised that you question the receipt I gave for income tax purposes. Especially, when this happens in such a whimsical way.
The parish priest often has to send two letters to the income tax officials, who then reply: All right, since you have accounted for your receipts, we shall accept them.
But then, consider all the steps that were required: a letter from the taxpayer to the income tax division, a letter from the taxpayer to his member of parliament, a letter of the member to the taxpayer, a letter of the member to the income tax division, another visit of the taxpayer to the parish priest, and then, another letter from the parish priest to the income tax division, and the department's reply to the taxpayer informing him that his receipts were justified, and all this for a $9.25 difference in the income tax assessment. This must have cost the government from $100 to $125, because the receipts for charitable donations were not accepted.
Why not accept these receipts if they are in due form? We have received a pile of letters from taxpayers who were dissatisfied.
I then decided to meet the income tax director. I was very well received but afterwards he did exactly the opposite of what he had promised me he would do. I said to the income tax director: When, in your opinion, charitable donation receipts are too high and you decide on an investigation, at least make a complete one. That is a legal requirement. Investigations by the income tax division cannot be complete as long as the investigators have not paid a visit to the taxpayer.
Some parish priests have told me that such visits are made no more than an hour before the evening rosary at the church, because the officials come from Quebec city and wish their stay in the Lake St. John area to be as short as possible. They arrive at any hour of the morning, afternoon or evening and say "We have prepared a list; give us the following information." The vicar is thus forced to do the investigation for the income tax officials. If he has signed a receipt for such and such
Income Tax Act
a person he must give the information on the spot and say: I do not know-
To allow people to act in such a way under that legislation is paramount to discrimination against the general public.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member again but it seems to me he is discussing the administration of the Income Tax Act, which is a responsibility of the Department of National Revenue. Up to this point he has not related his remarks to the resolution which is before us. I hope the hon. member will do that.

Mr. Chairman, once again I shall relate my remarks to the resolution. The relation between what I have to say and the resolution under consideration at this time is that the legislation before us is incomplete, that it lacks simplicity and is very difficult to understand for income tax inspectors and assessors. As a matter of fact, it is because they do not understand the act that such cases as those I have mentioned can happen.
By submitting specific cases to the Ministers of Finance and National Revenue, I hope to prove that they should introduce better prepared pieces of legislation than the one this house is discussing today if they want auditors to understand the provisions of the act.
That is the relevancy between what I say and the cases I quoted. I suggest those cases are so clear that they deserve consideration because it is a very important matter.
As a matter of fact, when legislation is passed and its provisions are ill applied or misinterpreted, we have a responsibility to see to it that justice is done to our electors who are the victims of the legislation we pass in this house.
This is, in my view, the relation between my remarks and the legislation we are called upon to vote.
It is a fine thing to ask us to pass legislation, but if they are improperly drafted and if most taxpayers complain about it because they cannot understand such legislation or make anything out of the intricacies of the law, we have a responsibility to say: do not bring forward any more budget resolutions or legislation with respect to income tax which are so drafted but see to it that the officials and the taxpayers can understand them.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that I have related my observations to the matter now before us and that I may go on.
Mr. Chairman, in the cases I mentioned, justice was finally rendered to certain indi-

Income Tax Act
viduals but only after a lengthy exchange of correspondence between the income tax department and the taxpayer, the parish priest and the member of parliament.
But if the inspector or the assessor had considered only what was asked for, if we had passed simpler, easier to understand, more explicit legislation, then we would not have faced such problems.
I have another case to illustrate very well what I am saying. It is the case of a taxpayer who said he was not allowed to deduct 75 per cent of his car expenditures because it was alleged that he did not have to use his car in his work. In the letter, the name of the assessor is mentioned. He is a Mr. Gingras. That man's name is often referred to in the letters received.
The taxpayer wrote to me as follows: I was a little tired after travelling more than 160 miles the day the inspector came in to my office. He came from Quebec city, and, as I said a while ago, he tried to get his work done as fast as possible.
And the taxpayer went on: although my day's work was done, and I had travelled 160 miles and seen several customers, the inspector barged into my office very rudely, asking me a thousand and one questions, accusing me of all kinds of things. I spoke to him a bit harshly, and then the inspector said to the secretary, and I have the name here, Mr. Gingras, that he would make me pay dearly for this lack of respect for a tax assessor.
Mr. Chairman, if we do not pass a law to bring those people to their senses, what is the use of our present legislation, apart from getting taxpayers into trouble?
Mr. Chairman, it is intended to have paid dearly any lack of respect for a tax assessor with whom it is impossible to discuss problems, who considers that we are all thieves and treats everyone accordingly.
Such are the legislative measures that we are being asked to pass in this house. The taxpayer also tells me: As I knew that my tax returns were legal, I did not worry much about this investigator who, in order to have his revenge gave me a new assessment for two years, and claimed $245.91 from me.
Mr. Chairman, this taxpayer unfortunately came to see me much too late, because had I known about that, I might have been able to put this Mr. Gingras in his place before today. The taxpayer handed me the letter so that I might use it.
He also tells me that when he received that $245.91 claim, instead of seeing a lawyer, which would probably have cost him twice as much, he offered to pay this amount at the rate of $25 per month. But Mr. Gingras was

up to his tricks again, and told the taxpayer that he had to pay the amount within a certain period of time.
That is another example showing how Quebec income tax officers act.
And I think that we are right when we ask for an investigation on the actions of these little dictators.
Another taxpayer writes me to ask where he stands. As a matter of fact, he is wondering if he will have to go to the income tax office in Quebec to swear that he actually gave so much to charities.
Mr. Chairman, those are somewhat extraordinary things. When it is said that an investigation was made, in most cases, there was none. In my opinion, there should be an investigation about the actions of those inspectors.
We ask only that an investigation be made when it is intended to reduce the amounts claimed by the taxpayers for charitable donations. The least they can do is for the officers and assessors to call on the taxpayers. In so doing, they may see both sides of the picture, they may obtain both versions. We also ask that they behave politely and not by saying: "We are above you, you are a gang of thieves."
Let them conduct their investigation politely when they refuse to accept the statements submitted. The investigation is not to be made in the income tax office; what we ask for is that the assessors or auditors visit the taxpayers themselves, instead of asking the taxpayers to go to the office. The Quebec district taxation office is located 135 miles from Jon-quiere and 175 miles from Mistassini, which is in the constituency of my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). In most cases, the officers tell the taxpayers: "If you are not satisfied, come to see us in Quebec city or lodge an appeal against our decision."
Mr. Chairman, I think if it is intended to pass legislation with respect to income tax, it must be drafted clearly and precisely, so that everybody may understand it. It is already hard enough to have to pay income tax. In fact, I believe the government grabs a sufficient share of the taxpayers' salary, it already digs deep enough into our pockets without entrusting the job to a bunch of rude and impertinent employees. Indeed, taxpayers have reason to complain, because their word always seems to be questioned with regard to receipts for charitable donations.
That is the situation in which everybody finds himself. We should keep in mind that a priest's or minister's task is not to give receipts. That is hardly his function. But if the taxpayer has no receipt from his parish priest, he has to pay taxes, even on the money he gave charitable institutions. It seems that

the parish priest is expected to do the work of a civil servant. When he signs a receipt, it seems that he sets everybody against himself: the taxpayer, the income tax department, everybody.
Mr. Chairman, the act is ill-conceived, and especially, the provision relating to receipts for charitable donations.
And today, we are asked to approve further income tax legislation. I think that if the minister wants to amend the Income Tax Act, he should amend the provision with regard to charitable donations, which is a source of trouble for each and every one of us. At least, we, in our district, receive a great number of complaints, and I suggest that the act be amended, instead of putting everybody in a difficult situation and abetting an existing trend, which is to incite people to cheat on their income tax return. I admit that there are some people who cheat, or try to cheat, but it is precisely that clause concerning charitable donation receipts, which encourages people to cheat or to obtain as many charitable donations receipts as possible from their parish priest, who is unwilling to make enemies. It may happen that a parish priest gives a receipt for an amount higher than the taxpayer's charities. But he does not have to squabble with his parishioners just to please the director of the income tax office or the inspector. Therefore, let us change the act. We have already made a suggestion along that line. I repeat it today and I ask the minister to move that amendment himself. In view of the fact that we are dealing with budget resolutions, I am ready to help him draft an amendment for which he will have all the merit and credit in Quebec. Let him move an amendment to the effect that-

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Saint John-Alberl) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of reviving the Canadian merchant marine.
Merchant Marine
He said: Mr. Speaker, this subject of a merchant marine has come before parliament on numerous occasions since world war II.
I hope to submit this afternoon that there are even more compelling reasons now for the government to revive, in the words of my motion, the Canadian merchant marine. In going over the previous debates one will find that perhaps the greatest champion of this cause in the house was the former minister of external affairs, Mr. Howard Green. When I came into the house it was my pleasure and honour to support a plea which he made on May 13, 1954, for the merchant marine. The reasons that we made that plea at that time still hold true today, and as I say I think are even more compelling. The ironical twist, Mr. Speaker, is that at that time, 1954, there were over 100 merchant ships. Today we have one Canadian-registered, deep sea vessel.
The arguments for this proposal were four in number. First of all there was the matter of defence; second, shipbuilding; then that of trained seamen; and fourth, the question of trade. I should like to deal with these four matters in light of present-day circumstances.
As far as defence is concerned, Mr. Speaker, while our commitments have changed somewhat we are still in the business of naval escorting. If we have no merchant ships to escort, then what will our navy do in time of war? I seriously suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the experience of the last war when we pooled our merchant ships should be a lesson to us at the present time. We sat down at the bargaining table, but those who had the ships could of course bargain the best and have their say. The piper plays the tune, as it were, and those who do not have a merchant fleet to back up their words at the conference table lose out.
Another argument made quite frequently is that today we need more air transport than naval transport. I suggest that this may be true in the first instance, but a recent article in the magazine "Crowsnest", April issue, demonstrates very clearly that while air transport may be required for our combat-readied troops, we have to follow up with naval transport immediately afterwards to supply materials and even fuel for the aircraft. So I think from a military prestige standpoint we can still justify the need for a merchant marine.
Then reference was made in the previous debate, as I said, to shipbuilding. A very interesting brief was presented to the federal cabinet recently by the shipyard workers of Canada, in which they pointed out in clearcut fashion the present need for a merchant marine. They said that if we did not need our

Merchant Marine
own ships, then we should not be in the shipbuilding business. Canadian ownership would assist the shipbuilding yards to a degree unprecedented in our history. They further pointed out that with the scrapping of the frigate program the yards are in a serious transformation stage, and the $400 or $500 million which was released by the cut in naval expenditures could be used to assist the construction of a Canadian merchant marine.
Then there is the question of trained seamen. We all know the difficulties which we encountered during the last war through the lack of trained seamen. I suggest that we in this nation need to look to the future. We had over 7,000 trained seamen in 1945; now there are less than 100. The sea would be a worthwhile occupation for Canadian youth to follow. They would know where they fit into the future, and this could be part of a naval or merchant marine program. We do train seamen for the Canadian coastguard service and for Department of Transport vessels on the northern service, and this training could be tied in with that for a privately-owned merchant marine.
The last point of significance which was made in the debate ten years ago still has validity today, and I suggest it is even more convincing. It concerns the matter of trade.
We are trading to an increasing extent. Our exports are going up all the time. Recently we saw an example of our need for a merchant marine in that our wheat has been shipped both to China and Russia in the bottoms of ships of other countries. This is why it is imperative that we move now to establish a merchant marine, because there is a great demand for the movement of bulk cargoes.
Two tables numbered I and IX which appeared in the brief submitted by the shipyard workers show, first of all, world and Canadian export trade as a percentage, as extracted from the marine engineering log, and second, the extent of foreign ships participating in the handling of Canadian overseas trade. These tables are in both French and English, but I would ask permission, Mr. Speaker, to have both these short tables which are extracted from official government records printed in Hansard in English at this point in the debate.
