Another example, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate the need for a Canadian merchant marine in the sphere of trade, is illustrated by recommendations made at the United Nations conference on trade and development. This was an extensive conference held in Geneva on March 25. One of the recommendations has particular significance, and it is as follows:
5. Ocean transport costs being so important to the trade of developing countries, they should be encouraged where feasible to set up their own merchant marines-when they do, it must be understood that they will have to indulge in the practice of "flag discrimination" to protect these fledgling enterprises.
Having examined the reasons for having a merchant marine it might be worth while to take a moment merely to outline what has taken place since 1945 to show where Canada has fallen down. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that after the second world war it was the policy of many of the smaller countries and states, such as Liberia and Panama, to provide a "flag of convenience", or to become what are called flag countries. This is a method of registration of a ship by a shipowner so as to escape tax liability in his country of origin. In many countries these shipowners suffered such a tax burden that they were forced to register their ships in countries like Panama or Liberia. As a consequence most countries took steps, through various methods such as tax concessions, subsidies or mortgages, to make it possible for their own shipowners to register ships at home and compete with these smaller nations. In other words, they placed their own shipowners in a competitive position. But Canada failed to do this, and for the life of me I cannot understand why we allowed our merchant fleet to dwindle since 1945 almost to the point of non-existence.
There is no sense in reviewing the history of the matter. Various proposals have been put forward from time to time. I am sure there are many recommendations and briefs which have been put before the Department of Transport and other departments which are worth while, and could form the basis of any shipbuilding scheme. I know from personal experience some of the difficulties of a fully socialized plan of ship operation, and I for one would have no part in any state ownership scheme which might be put forward. We all know the difficulties experienced by Canadian National Steamships, who were running ships to the West Indies.
I should first like to make the suggestion that whatever is done should be done now. There is enough authority and power in the Canadian Maritime Commission Act and regulations for us to carry out any method
Merchant Marine
we may have in mind to deal with this important matter. It is only necessary, as I suggested, to put our shipping industry in a position to be able to compete with those of other countries.
The second important thing to remember is that, whether this is done by government mortgage, by tax concessions or other forms of assistance, it must be long term to be fair to all-shipowners, seamen, shipyard workers and even the Canadian people. It may be necessary to go even further and to restrict our exports and imports, if possible, to Canadian bottoms as has been done by the United States. But let us be fair to everyone. Let us be long term in our suggestions and recommendations and let us not have a tragic abandonment of our merchant marine as we had in 1945.
I do not wish to speak long. I suggest that these are the advantages of a revived Canadian owned, operated and manned deep sea merchant marine. First of all, it would give new opportunities to thousands of young Canadians who would follow the sea as a lifetime profession. Second, it would stimulate Canadian shipbuilding in the tough, competitive world of today. Third, it would bring new dollars to our economy and reduce our balance of payments problems. Instead of sharing present shipowners' revenues outside of Canada, the earnings would all be distributed within our own economy. Fourth, it would give Canada greater control over import and export traffic. It would stabilize our shipping costs and bring us into the picture in chartering, insurance and even the direction of shipping. Fifth, it would provide greater prestige and bargaining power in trade negotiations with the newly developing countries. Last, it would mean that we would have available, having in mind present defence commitments, a merchant fleet for both the supply and transport of troops.
Canada is a vast and complex country. Because of our geography we have found it necessary from time to time to subsidize many of our services in the transportation field. Because of our sparse population we have also found it necessary to come forward with assistance on occasion to agriculture and some of our other basic industries. We have one of the longest and most rugged coastlines in the world, and it certainly is not wrong to think that we should assist in some way a Canadian owned merchant fleet that would bring us closer to the sea.
It would have a very healthy effect on our people. In my opinion we have become too insular in Canada. We are controlled from central Canada, and we seem to forget the wholesome sea is at our gates. We are, to put

Merchant Marine
it bluntly, a nation of landlubbers. A small investment such as I suggest, which would only amount to $3 million a year for about 25 ships, would once and for all enable us to take our place as a great trading nation with our own ships, our own seamen and the other supporting industrial services.
Let us have a decision now instead of waiting another 25 years. I do not know whether this matter should be referred to a committee. Possibly the railways and shipping committee could gather information that could be of great assistance in helping the government to make a decision. It might be that the matter could be referred to the banking and commerce committee. I think everybody agrees on the need of reviving our merchant marine. It is a matter of deciding the best financial method of doing so. I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has many duties. His portfolio is a most diverse one. He cannot hope to cope with all his problems overnight, but he should try to direct his attention to one matter at a time. The former minister of transport, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), in a commend-ably statesmanlike fashion dealt with shipbuilding. He brought forward the subsidy plan which enabled us to build our coastal ships, and this helped the industry for a considerable period. I suggest to the Minister of Transport that he should act at once by taking the matter of reviving our merchant marine under immediate consideration, and come forward with a program that will benefit the entire economy.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have this opportunity to take part in the present debate, especially to deal with the establishment of a merchant marine, a project which I think would be feasible and economical in a country such as ours.
Many people today talk about small industries and say that, in Canada, we should establish and promote the establishment of small industries. That is true, but before doing that, we should keep and try to improve those we already have. I feel the time has come to examine the possibility of establishing a merchant marine. There are several good reasons for such a project, and here are the main ones: 1. Canada is one of the largest exporters in the world, but its exports to countries other than the United States are carried in ships of foreign registry.
2. A Canadian merchant marine would open many markets to Canadian shipyards, both for shipbuilding and repairs, and at the same time it would put our Canadian labour force to work on the equipment required for those ships.

3.	Canadian shipyards having no merchant marine to supply and serve in Canada labour under a serious handicap.
4.	The earnings of the Canadian merchant marine would reduce our balance of payments.
Present conditions, although quite unfavourable to the development of a Canadian oceangoing fleet, are not necessarily permanent, and this matter should be examined from time to time, as technical changes occur.
The application of automation to shipping is increasing from day to day. This could lessen the dispute about the wages of Canadian seamen abroad and enable to diversify our operations in the future.
I now take the liberty, Mr. Speaker, of referring to the brief submitted by the national trade union and the Canadian Congress of Labour to the cabinet; there are very few countries which have a more direct interest in shipping than Canada. Almost 16 per cent of our gross national product of $40.4 billion, that is $6.4 billion, is derived from exports. From 1957 to 1962, our exports accounted for 5 per cent of total world exports. Except for the world trade in oil, considering only the shipping trade of solid goods, Canada's share is even higher: 9.6 per cent in 1961.
In the face of such a situation, the condition of our merchant marine is disastrous: we only have one trading ship under Canadian registry the SS Federal Pioneer, of 10,000 tons built during the war. Such a situation cannot prevail without definitely being prejudicial to our commercial position in the world.
This is more pitiful since Canada has a shipping tradition of which it can be proud. After 1867, our country ranked fourth among the countries having a merchant marine. As shipbuilders, we ranked third during the second world war, immediately after the United States and Great Britain.
A modern merchant marine would guarantee to our country the development of our external trade and actively contribute to increase our exports.
It would provide jobs for thousands of Canadians. It would bring about the technical development of an important segment of our heavy industry. It would bring additional revenue to several related industries and to various localities. Finally, it would soon contribute to solve one of our main economic problems: The chronic imbalance of our international payments. We have the required capital, as well as the human and material resources available. At this stage, the federal government should reach a prompt decision.
Canadian shipments to foreign countries have reached 60.3 million tons in 1962, or a 12 per cent increase compared to the previous year. This rising trend is being maintained.

For the first five months of 1963, there is a 6 per cent increase, compared to the corresponding period in 1962.
Iron ore comes first with 24.3 million tons, followed by wheat (9 million tons), gypsum (4.1 million tons), lumber and timber (3 million tons).
Those three types of shipments totalled 22.1 million tons. The transportation of those three products alone required a fleet of 40 ships of 25,000 tons each, at the rate of two trips a month.
During 1963, the total volume of shipments handled in Canadian ports was higher than in any previous year and exceeded by 8 per cent the record reached in 1961.
According to 28th annual report of the national harbours board tabled in parliament by the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, Minister of Transport, who is responsible for the board, those ports have known an unprecedented activity as well as a record operating income.
Such increased activity prevailed in all the harbours coming under the board which administers the Halifax, St. John's, Chicoutimi, Quebec, Three Rivers, Montreal, Churchill and Vancouver harbours as well as the grain elevators in Prescott and Port Col-borne.
Mr. Speaker, shipping has topped all previous records. The Canadian national harbours have handled a surplus of 66 million tons of freight, namely a 10 per cent increase above the 1962 volume.
Exports have increased by nearly 24 per cent compared to last year, when imports remained about the same as in 1962. Domestic traffic, upon arrival, increased by 12 per cent and domestic traffic, upon departure, by nearly 1 per cent.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker:
1.	It is not surprising that shipyards are specialized plants which must rely on the skills patiently acquired by steelworkers, welders, coppersmiths, electricians, carpenters, cabinet-makers, modelmakers, riggers, tinsmiths and others.
Such skills must be kept continuously occupied in shipbuilding, if we want to avoid that such a mine of talents be wasted and scattered. Shipyards are tottering when such skills remain idle. They make headway and spread economic development throughout the country when farsighted maritime nations see to it that their expert teams work at their main job, building and repairing ships.
2.	In the near future, a steel industry will be established in Quebec, which will increase considerably our needs with regard to water transportation.
3.	There was a considerable increase in winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river,
Merchant Marine
according to the report published in March 1964 by the board of industry and commerce of Metropolitan Quebec Inc., whose main object is to supply the industry and trade of the economic region of Quebec with a supplementary service that might contribute to their development.
I take the liberty of quoting a few figures from the newspaper Le Soleil:
Statistics on shipbuilding up to 1961 have just been released. The number of shipyard workers dropped from 18,577 in 1957 to 14,848 in 1961. Quebec had the largest labour force, that is 8,005 in 1957 and 6,168 in 1961, next came British Columbia with employment figures of 5,001 and 2,946 workers, respectively...
In 1961, the gross value of production amounted to $136,629,459, Quebec getting $61,262,965 of it. Most orders are placed by the federal government.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say that the government should take steps to stabilize employment in our shipyards and I think that it could do it best by setting up a merchant marine as soon as possible. I suggest, therefore, that the motion be referred to a committee for study.
In short, here are a few most urgent recommendations that I wish to submit to the government.
1.	That jurisdiction over the coastal trade be extended to the Belle Isle strait, Newfoundland being a Canadian province.
2.	That the ships be built, repaired and registered in Canada and have their home ports here.
3.	That the 33J per cent subsidies be covered by permanent legislation and not by orders in council, as at the present time.
4.	That shipyards be regulated by federal legislation, mainly for the following reasons:
(a)	60 per cent of shipbuilding involve contracts with the federal government.
(b)	The inspection is carried out by the federal government.
(c)	Shipbuilding is a national industry.
(d)	The abovementioned subsidies are granted by the federal government. Hence shipping will be covered by federal legislation on coastal trade and licences will be delivered by the Department of Transport.
5.	That a shipbuilding commission be set up to regulate Canadian shipyards. The commission could establish equitable plans for each area. In brief, for such a study, I respectfully suggest that the government should set up a parliamentary committee on coastal shipping in order that the recommendations made in the 1957 report be implemented.

Mr. Speaker, as member for a riding bordering on the majestic Saguenay, one of the most beautiful rivers in the world, it is natural that

Merchant Marine
I should be keenly interested in the establishment of a merchant marine and harbour improvements.
Our area is fortunate in that private undertakings have been able to organize themselves and establish their own shipping industry, because we would have been deprived altogether along that line. There is, for instance the Saguenay Terminal, which has its home port in Port Alfred and owns a sizeable fleet, that is about 100 ships which bring in raw materials from South America and Africa and export products manufactured in the Saguenay area, especially paper and aluminium.
That is not enough, however, and it does not meet present needs not only in my district but throughout the country. It must be remembered that shipbuilding was the first industry of its kind in Canada. If you read the economic history of our country you will see that the first industry established here was a shipyard. We have the advantage of being almost surrounded by water; we have oceans at the north, east and west and the majestic St. Lawrence and the great lakes to the south. However, we have no merchant marine to ply those waters. That is truly amazing on the part of a country with a population of nearly 20 million people.
We have shipyards and I know that the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) is keenly interested in this matter. He may have strong arguments but I should like to stress one point, the financial element. In spite of the numerous arguments he invoked, the member failed to show the need for shipbuilding. Indeed, the saddest point of all is that the government does not have the funds at present to build ships.
It is faced with the following problem: the people are overtaxed and still we are being asked for money for shipbuilding.
Here, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) for having raised this question of major importance for the Canadian economy. However, if concrete proposals enabling us to build ships are not brought down, all efforts will be of no avail. In fact, we have the necessary materials and labour, and we have well organized shipyards, but the funniest part of it all is that we lack the money. By the way, what is money? In itself, it is merely a means of acquiring property. Some economists call it a certificate to get goods.
As potential, we have the Bank of Canada, which is the people's bank, the nation's bank, and we are not using that potential, that power which could capitalize this country's assets. We could, considering that point of view, create thousands of new jobs in this

country, we could train our young people and we would become much more interested, as our economy would be more prosperous.
On the other hand, if we consider the way money is being spent on social assistance- millions are being spent annually on social assistance of some kind-we cannot but conclude that instead of distributing money for nothing, it would be better to use it to build ships in which to carry our products to other countries and to bring back those products we need.
When we look upon small countries, such as Norway and Sweden and many others that have large fleets, we surely have cause for reflection. I often see in Chicoutimi harbour ships which come all the way from Sweden or Norway. As a matter of fact, it is on account of these ships coming in from far away countries that we benefit from a number of Canadians of foreign origin who are now assimilated to the French Canadians but whose origin is Norwegian, Swedish, even Finnish. These sailors discovered that we have a magnificent country, liked it, and have remained with us.
It has been established that shipping by waterway from Canada to foreign countries has increased considerably in 1962, that is, by 12 per cent.
Now that we want to extend Canada's export markets, perspectives seem tremendous. In the course of this week, and according to what I was told, I will probably have the opportunity, of introducing my Bill No. C-24, an Act to amend the Bank of Canada Act. If the house sees fit to pass that bill, we will then be able to increase our exports considerably and we will have to build a fleet of ships to sail the seven seas; we will then be able to do business with all those countries enjoying a relatively stable economy, a relatively stable government, from whom we could accept non convertible currencies. We may then also be able to increase our exports considerably.
Keeping all those countries in mind, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say in conclusion that Canada, after all, is an exporting country. The same can be said of my own Saguenay region, because if it were not for our exports nobody could earn a living there. All the industries of my region export 90, 95 and even 98 per cent of their production.
It is also the case with most of our large Canadian industries. Therefore, shipbuilding is of the utmost importance, but let us, by all means, open our eyes and see where we can obtain capital. A merchant marine will not be built by overtaxing people, but by tapping available sources of funds. We have the advantage of having the report of the royal commission on banking and finance. I

did not have the time to look it over personally to see whether it contained concrete solutions to boost our economy. However, let us not forget that conditions now are not what they were 50 or 100 years ago. Times have changed and we have to take that evolution into account. When we can monetize our own improvements, we will be able to monetize the Canadian potential, to monetize, in the long run, our national resources, but, in order to do that, it is imperative that we build a merchant marine.
The financial system has changed and we can consider ourselves in a position to benefit from our wealth; from Canada's potential and from our natural resources. To achieve this goal, we must without fail set up a merchant marine of which Canada would be proud and which would allow the country to assert itself when we have a flag worthy of our country.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration is a very important one. It is a pity that it was not introduced by the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) when his party was on the other side of the house. When the hon. members belong to the party in power, they seem to remain idle, but when they are in the opposition, they become very aggressive.
In 1962, in connection with coastal shipping in Canada, the volume of goods carried in the inland waters of the St. Lawrence including the great lakes reached 43,375,648 tons. Ninety seven English ships not registered in Canada and three foreign ones engaged in coastal shipping with a temporary licence issued by the Minister of Transport were in operation in 1962.
Five million, 8 hundred and 99 thousand, 9 hundred tons, that is 13.6 per cent of the total coasting trade for 1962, have been shipped on vessels registered outside Canada. During the same year, such vessels carried: all British Columbia timber to harbours of eastern Canada; 94 per cent of limestone from Colborne to Clarkson; 90 per cent of ilmenite from Havre St-Pierre to Sorel; about 87 per cent of gypsum from Little Narrows to Montreal; over 50 per cent of iron ore from Wabana to Sydney; 65 per cent of the coal shipped from Sydney; 44 per cent of the iron ore shipped from Seven Islands.
That gives you an idea of the importance for our merchant marine, namely ships registered and built in Canada, to see that they possess the exclusive right of an inshore freight service or at least in the St. Lawrence inland waters.
It would also assist greatly the Canadian shipyards which, this way, could get contracts
Merchant Marine
for the construction of boats which undertake exclusively that inshore service.
Our shipyards play a great part in the economic life of the Quebec area. They are among the most important employers, giving work to a great number of workers and specialized technicians who all receive salaries ranging among the highest in the Quebec area.
In addition, shipbuilding benefits the entire Canadian economy. The greater part of the materials used in shipbuilding are manufactured and processed in Canada. Steel, engines, electrical equipment and interior decorating materials are mostly manufactured in Canada and their manufacture provides jobs to a great number of Canadian workers whose earnings benefit the whole of our economy.
The hon. member for Three Rivers, minister of transport in the previous government, announced on May 12, 1961 that the Canadian government intended to introduce a legislation which would restrict coastal shipping to ships registered in Canada. On November 12, 1962, the hon. member reaffirmed his government's intention to amend the legislation so as to give effect to that proposal from May 12, 1961.
On June 13, 1963, the President of the Privy Council, who was minister of transport during the last session, has stated anew that the present government still intends to amend the legislation in order to reserve the coastal trade for Canadian ships.
Many foreign ships, including those of the United States, Australia, Italy, France, Greece and Western Germany reserve the coastal trade for ships flying the flag of their respective country.
Canada is fully justified to pass such a measure, for is could help greatly the economy and give employment to workers that could build ships as well as to crews of ships flying the Canadian flag.
About 15 days ago, the national federation of metallurgy submitted to the federal cabinet a brief asking that a Canadian merchant marine be set up. That brief contained a letter from the late Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, former minister of veterans affairs-it goes back to June 4, 1945, that is 20 years ago- addressed to the Vancouver shipyard workers:
On behalf of the Canadian government, I wish to express to you Canada's appreciation for your contribution to victory. The workers of British Columbia, using new techniques acquired since the beginning of the war, built ships totalling three million tons: 53 warships, 231 transport ships-for a total cost of $500 million, half of which was paid in salaries locally; 65 ships are under construction. When you started, 90 per cent of the materials were imported. At the present time, 90 per cent are Canadian made, and this ensures the continued existence of our shipbuilding industry.
Thanks to your competence, your zeal and your energy, in other words, thanks to you, workers, Vancouver's maritime industry is unparalleled from the point of view both of equality and production

Merchant Marine
Canada is grateful to you and assure you that your competence and your skills will be necessary for future tasks-
And here, Mr. Speaker, is the most important part of the letter written 20 years ago:
Let us not repeat past mistakes. The present government believes that Canada's shipbuilding industry is here to stay.
The navy and the merchant marine you have built up will be retained and developed. The ships you have built will transport Canadian products to the four comers of the world thus creating employment and opportunities for Canadian workers.
The present government has set forth and is now carrying out policies to ensure employment and to expand our trade in the post-war era. Your skill will be needed in the shipyards and in the new industries which will be set up through our expanding trade.
The government which has prepared and launched this vast shipbuilding program in Vancouver requests your help to carry out the projects it has devised to ensure that you are employed in the trades in which you have become so highly skilled.
Sincerely yours,
Ian A. Mackenzie,
Minister of Veterans' Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, that letter was written 20 years ago. It is being said that the present government has prepared plans which it is now carrying out, but I believe that those plans were put aboard a destroyer and that they sank to the bottom of the ocean.
Now, on page 6 of that brief, one can find the following lines:
That state of affairs is all the more distressing since Canada has a maritime tradition she can be rightly proud of. During the years following 1867, this country came fourth among the countries having a merchant marine. We came third as shipbuilders during the last war, next to the United States and Great Britain.
What is possible during war time is also feasible during peacetime for constructive purposes. The setting up of a modem merchant marine would guarantee the expansion of our foreign trade and would contribute actively to the increase of our exports. It would provide employment to thousands of Canadians and bring about the technical renovation of a major sector of our heavy industry. It would provide additional revenue to several related industries and to various localities. Finally, it would provide a prompt solution to one of our major economic problems, that is the chronic deficit of our balance of international payments.
And the same brief continues as follows:
We have at our disposal the capital and the human and material resources we need. At this stage, the federal government must make a decision, and it must act right now.
A while ago, I noticed that the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) mentioned goods such as iron ore, wheat and lumber, whose shipping alone would keep going a fleet of 40 ships.

And again, in the same brief, the shipping of iron ore, wheat and lumber is mentioned. Here is what it says:
These three types of shiploads make a total of 22.1 million tons. The shipping alone of these three kinds of goods would require a fleet of 40 ships of 25,000 tons each, at the rate of two trips monthly.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this is an area which should not be disregarded by hon. members.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Levis for having supported the resolution. I think that the time has come for the government to act.
Mr. Speaker, putting the merchant marine back into service in Canada is a necessity for our Canadian economy. The coastal trade for instance should be more important in Canada than in any other country, considering our geographical position, and the great extent of our coastal and interior waters.
The great lakes, are, after all, inland seas. The coastal trade helps to train sailors and shipowners. If the existing legislation is maintained, which tolerates an almost disloyal competition, and forces our shipowners, whose vessels engage in the coastal trade, to struggle under exceptionally difficult conditions, they will be unable to stand up to that competition, and a crisis will ensue which will be difficult for Canada to overcome.
Our coastal waters could very well be invaded by ships registered anywhere in the commonwealth, except in Canada.
That is why it is high time for Canada to have her own merchant navy. This could also keep that shipping revenue in Canada, which would help maintain a favourable balance of payments in our international trade.

Over the years I have always been in favour of Canada having a merchant marine. I am therefore very much in support of the principle of the motion which is now before us.
However, this is one of the most complicated matters with which we could be asked to deal. A great many of us remember the time when Canada did have a merchant marine, and a good one. Because of government policy, or perhaps because of competition, we lost our merchant fleet. Therefore, when we consider in principle building another one we should take into consideration the reasons why we lost our merchant marine, and the difficulties which would face the establishment of a new one. There is the question of the cost of the ships and of the existence of a profitable contractual basis for shipowners, shipbuilders and the union. There is the question of the standardization of costs in the

operation. There are so many imponderables that this is a matter which could not be discussed in one hour in this house.
My only purpose in rising is to say that I have always been in favour of the re-establishment of a Canadian merchant marine. I believe that as an export nation and with the shore line we have on the Atlantic, the Pacific and the great lakes, we are required to have a merchant marine; but I also believe that in order to make certain that we bring into being a new merchant marine of the most modern, efficient and functional nature, it requires a great deal of study and will require commitments by those who build and those who operate. Therefore, sir, I most certainly hope that in the furtherance of the principle and the belief that we should have a merchant marine, this motion will be referred to a committee of the House of Commons for a full and continuing study, with a report being brought back to the house.

Mr. Speaker, with the wording of the notice of motion before us, one cannot quarrel in any respect, depending of course on how one may interpret it. It says:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of reviving the Canadian merchant marine.
In a general sense I say that Canada needs to keep itself informed in any field of economic activity, whether it be in the production of goods, the production of services or in the utilization of its skills in the production of ships for the carrier trade of the world. Canada lives today in a state of international economic circumstances that challenges our imagination as to what course we should choose for the future. Indeed, there is very little in the past to guide us except to remind us of events that may have been happy ones, or sometimes unhappy ones. Our shipbuilders learned their skills in the past. We have inherited this ability to construct ships in Canada that were much needed, sorely needed indeed, a few years ago during world war II, as they were also needed in world war I. So that when you approach the reasons why a nation should undertake to promote a particular economic activity, you find very often reasons for undertaking such proposals that do not appear on the surface when you first examine the question. I have heard some say quickly, and with apparent good reason and common sense, that if we build a merchant fleet, man it and endeavour to develop cargoes for these ships to the international ports of the world, we may very well lose some of our export trade because those foreign countries who derive foreign exchange from the
Merchant Marine
carrier trade will not have the wherewithal with which to purchase our particular goods. This is a superficial argument and I think that when very close examination is given to it, it will not stand up in this age of multilateral trade and great strivings to bring nations of the world into freer relationships in trading, the production of their goods and services with each other.
What we are looking for throughout the world, with the exploding population that we have, is an expansion of production to meet the total world needs, and no longer can we hide our heads in the sand, like the ostrich, and hope that world events will not touch us. It is inevitable that they will. It seems to me that in our pursuit of national economic goals, which we are told by those who are skilful in these fields are full employment, price stability, maximum multilateral trade and steady growth of our national production-these are the standard words that are used-surely we must, through education and experience, also remember that a great asset which we have is the skill of our people in the production of goods, and one of those great skills is the production of ships. I think that Canada would indeed suffer greatly, if it has not already suffered, by its unwillingness to at least make some degree of investment in the maintenance of a merchant marine.
There is no doubt whatsoever that to all of us in the Atlantic provinces and many others it seems that Canada should not exist without ships of this nation traversing the oceans of the world. We have long believed this was part of our development in the first place. Sir Samuel Cunard thought so many years ago, and he was able to meet the competition in those days. Surely to goodness we can find for ourselves some share of the carrier service internationally in this year 1964, and carrying on in the future. I subscribe to the view that a Canadian merchant navy will provide a splendid opportunity for young Canadians to have a career in the trading services, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) pointed out a short time ago.
I believe that the maintenance of our skills in shipbuilding will be required by Canada to hold its place in the changing pattern of international trade and commerce. I believe, also, that we need to utilize all our capabilities in the field of production and should be ready to meet with a very flexible capability any changes that are bound to occur. In the past decade the rebuilt and modernized economies of other countries have become increasingly vigorous and imaginative. Those countries I believe have managed to obtain for

Income Tax Act
themselves a share of the international carrier trade, and even without it they would still have maintained their trading patterns with Canada.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:

(a)	that is a university, college or other educational institution providing courses at a postsecondary school level,
(b)	that is a school operated by or on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province, a municipality in Canada, or a municipal or public body performing a function of government in Canada,

if the tuition fees paid by the taxpayer for the year exceed $25.
2.	That for the 1964 and subsequent taxation years a dependant in respect of whom a taxpayer may deduct an amount not exceeding $550 in computing his taxable income shall include a taxpayer's brother or sister who was 21 years of age or over and in full time attendance at a school or university.

That the period commencing on December 5, 1963 within which a new manufacturing or processing business must have commenced manufacturing or processing in reasonable commercial quantities in a designated area in order to obtain a certificate for the purposes of section 71A of the act be extended to March 31, 1967.

5.	That where at a time when an area was a designated area a business has been certified to be a new manufacturing or processing business, or an application has been made in writing to the Minister of Industry by a taxpayer in respect of a business that upon the fulfilment of specified conditions would be certified to be a new manufacturing or processing business in the designated area, that area, notwithstanding that it may no longer be a designated area, shall for the purpose of the application of section 71A of the act to that particular business continue to be a designated area.

9.	That for the 1964 and subsequent taxation years the period of 60 days from the end of a year within which an employer may pay an amount to or under a registered pension fund or plan in respect of services rendered by his employees be increased to 120 days.
10.	That for the 1964 and subsequent taxation years it be made clear that any amount received by an employer upon the winding up or reorganization of a pension fund or plan shall be included in his income.
11. Mr. Chairman, in starting my remarks tonight perhaps you will allow me to offer congratulations to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Kelly), who made a great effort and played so well to assist his team in winning the Stanley cup. I think he deserves to be congratulated because he is a gentleman on the ice, as well as a very good player.

Mr. Chairman, at the close of my remarks this afternoon, I referred to a necessary change in the Income Tax Act, especially with regard to receipts for charitable donations, which may be included in the income tax return for deduction purposes.
This act needs to be changed and I believe everybody here will agree. Efforts must be made to amend this part of the Income Tax Act, but until the said act is amended, it seems to me rather strict recommendations; should be made to the Quebec taxation officers in order that they themselves may be the first to respect the legislation we voted in this house, and that they stop harassing; the taxpayers as they do at the present time.
We already have a suggestion to amend this legislation and it should be included in the budget resolutions. Here is this suggestion: For the first $3,000 taxable income, there should be an automatic deduction of 10 per cent for charitable donations, without, receipts being required; for the next $2,000*

or $3,000, the percentage may be 1\ per cent, and for the next $1,000 or $2,000, it may be reduced to 5 per cent.
In the case of the companies, this measure would not be as necessary since unit payments of each company are higher than those of individuals and these companies are in a better position-they have accountants, a bookkeeping service specializing in taxation settlements-to meet these Income Tax Act provisions.
But in the case of individuals, it is urgent to amend the act. We must put an end to the violation of the law, as I have shown this afternoon by striking and typical cases, by officials of the tax department and especially to unsatisfactory investigations, where the taxpayers are not consulted and are often treated with scorn.
Mr. Chairman, we are ready to pass amendments to the tax act, especially in order to cut taxes. But we think that those amendments are also needed and we ask the minister to deal with them as soon as possible.
After the study in committee of those resolutions, a bill will be put before us in order that we may pass it. In my opinion, the minister should make an effort so that when the bill on budget resolutions is introduced this year, the Income Tax Act will be amended in order to allow a standard reduction for charity purposes for all taxpayers, without having to supply receipts. We would thus eliminate the continuous complaints that we now receive. May I tell you, Mr. Chairman, that we receive every week dozens of complaints from taxpayers about the discriminatory and dictatorial ways of tax inspectors and assessors.
May the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue make an effort as soon as possible to improve this legislation accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I might clear up one or two points which have been raised, mainly on paragraph 1, because I think it would be easier to answer some of the other questions relating to the following paragraphs when we come to them. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, in discussing the proposed exemption for students' fees, raised the question of textbooks, and also various other items of expense incurred by certain individuals in the process of earning their income. This is one of the questions which I have no doubt- in fact I am sure-is being studied carefully by the royal commission on taxation. It is a very difficult and complicated question, and it seemed to me that as the report of the commission will be available some time this
Income Tax Act
fall we should wait until we receive it, before reaching a conclusion on that particular point.
The hon. member for Lapointe has dealt with a question which is not covered by these resolutions, but with the indulgence of the committee perhaps I might be allowed to make a brief comment with regard to it. He has talked about the difficult question of deductions for charitable donations and the difficulties which the administration of this problem has caused both in his province and in other provinces of Canada. This matter was raised at some length and in some detail by various hon. members last fall, and I can assure all hon. members that since then I have given considerable thought and consideration to this problem. I discussed it on many occasions with our late colleague, the then minister of national revenue, who was very concerned to see that this difficulty is resolved. However, as I said in my budget speech, we came to the conclusion that with the resources at our disposal and with the time available I was not prepared to make a recommendation which I felt would meet all of the difficulties which had been raised.
Therefore the matter was referred specifically and directly to the royal commission on taxation, and the chairman was asked, with the advantages of his not inconsiderable research staff and the special qualifications of the members of his commission, whether he would address himself to this particular problem and give us his commission's best judgment on how to resolve it. As I said when the budget was brought down, that is where the matter stands. It has certainly not been ignored by the government; we are taking it seriously, but we think we should take advantage of the machinery which is now available and which will not always be available- because the commission expects to wind up its operations this fall-to make a careful study of this question.
I can assure the hon. member for Lapointe that his point concerning the administration of individual income tax offices was one which was carefully noted by the previous minister of national revenue, and I can assure him that his remarks will be equally noted and seriously considered by the present minister. Further than that I do not think I should go; it would be straying away from the resolution which is before us. I think I have answered the questions that have been raised so far with regard to paragraph 1, and perhaps I might deal with the others when we come to the respective paragraphs.

Mr. Chairman, since we are discussing the budget resolution concerning the Income Tax Act, it is in order to make certain comments on taxation. The resolution was set forth in the following terms:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act-
To legislate some specific things, among others.
I feel I must urge the minister at this time to consider the pressing need for a reduction of taxes in general and especially personal income tax which, in the opinion of many of our country's economists, has reached a level which is beyond all reason and might be called confiscatory.
I know that the minister may answer me as he did before. He will say that he cannot, at this stage, consider reducing taxes because a commission is now studying the whole Canadian taxation system and nothing can be changed in the system until that commission has submitted its report.
It may well be, Mr. Chairman, that after the commission has presented its report, the minister will then take that opportunity, in order to continue to temporize, to say that the report must now be fully considered.
You can see where that will lead us. It will lead us to a long period of inaction and stagnation. For it is a recognized fact that the fiscal and taxation structure in our country is precluding those very results the minister is hoping for, that is, an expansion of the economy and the economic activity in this country.
The Minister of Finance might say that the members on this side of the House do not seem to agree on the advisability of reducing taxes. As a matter of fact, the minister did say that-he even attempted to make me contradict my colleague, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), by saying that he was against a reduction of taxes while others like myself, had spoken in favour of a certain reduction.

Well, I think that the Minister of Finance is attempting to spread confusion unduly as regards this question, which is however very clear. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, did say at a certain time, during one of our party's conventions, that he was against a particular reduction, that is to a resolution which would compel our party, once it would become the government, for it will soon be in power again, to reduce taxes in a particular sector and by a certain amount.
Such a stand is logical, of course, as we cannot-and the Minister of Finance will agree-impose specific measures on a minister of finance, who should be entirely free to determine what taxes that should be reduced, which ones should be maintained and which ones should be repealed. We all agree on that point but we, on this side of the house, sincerely feel that in general taxes should be reduced immediately.
If we take that attitude it is because we believe in fiscal responsibility. The minister may claim that, regardless of what some people say, American taxpayers are more heavily assessed than their Canadian counterparts. Such a contention must be examined closely and distinctions have to be made. A Canadian financial paper, the Financial Post of Toronto has made a proper comparison between American and Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Chairman, I hope you will not call me to order because, as I said at the outset of my remarks, we are considering the Income Tax Act and the amendments to be made to it. And we say that these amendments must tend to reduce taxes, so as to make it possible for the Canadian industry to shake off its shackles, which is impossible as long as the government will not assume energetically its responsibilities in that field.
As I was saying, the United States did not wait for the findings of a commission of inquiry or a similar commission to cut taxes substantially. That cut will range between $11 and $12 billion. You must admit that a cut of $11.5 billion is quite extraordinary. Such a step was taken because the United States realized that it was the only way to step up the economic expansion and, if need be, to free the capital needed to increase consumption and the industrial, commercial and financial activity of the country in general.
It could be done, because they knew at the same time how to take strong measures in order to reduce government expenditures. That is the reason why, and the minister is quite aware of it, in the current United States budget, a $3 billion cut in government expenditures has been forecast. But here, what do we do? It is stated with an emotion which

I do not think is genuine or certainly with an obvious lack of logic, that economic activity must be stepped up.
However, taxation deprives the taxpayers of gains they could have reinvested in production. In fact, it is like an octopus reaching with its arms in every direction and devouring anything that gets in its way. The government increases its control over everybody's income by its fiscal policy. Thus, the Minister of Finance has to collect the necessary revenue in order to pay the increasing governmental expenditures. His attitude is surely inconsistent. If he does not believe me, he only has to consider the financial reports throughout the country and the editorials in newspapers such as the Financial Post and the Financial Times. Every responsible paper in the country does not hesitate to show in very strong terms the inconsistency of the minister's attitude and, at the same time, of the government's position.
I shall refer again to the example of two average taxpayers, one living in Canada, and the other in the United States, both earning a salary of $10,000 a year. What is the situation of both taxpayers in the federal taxation field? The American will pay $1,799 in federal income tax while the Canadian taxpayer will pay $1,664. This means that mathematically, as far as figures are concerned the American wage earner has a net income of $8,201 and the Canadian wage earner a net income of $8,336, that is the Canadian will get about $135 more than the American wage earner, after deduction of the federal income tax.
But such is not the real situation. It must be remembered that in general, wages in United States are much higher than in Canada for similar jobs or trades. When the average American wage earner gets $10,000 per year to perform a certain type of work, his Canadian counterpart who does the same work, according to the data compiled by the Financial Post of March 21, 1964, gets only $7,500. So there is a wide difference between the salary of the American taxpayer, whether he is a plumber, an electrician or an unskilled labourer, and that of the Canadian taxpayer. Before income tax deductions, there is already a difference of $2,500 in salary and, after tax deduction, the average American still has $8,201 but the Canadian only has $6,462 left. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian taxpayer doing the same kind of work as the American taxpayer gets about $2,000 less than his counterpart.
And the disparity is still wider because the American is paid in American dollars, which is normal; while the Canadian is paid in Canadian dollars which are at a discount;
Income Tax Act
therefore when the American taxpayer receives $8,857, the Canadian taxpayer receives only $6,462. Then the gap is about $2,400. And one must also consider that American dollars have more purchasing power than Canadian dollars. It is generally agreed that the American taxpayer pays less for consumer goods than the Canadian taxpayer.
Therefore, Canadian taxpayers are clearly at a disadvantage compared with the Americans. And yet, the minister draws a comparison with the American taxpayer to deprive the poor Canadian taxpayers of the income tax cut they clearly need. In so doing he does not seem to consider the greater need we have in Canada for capital, that is, for savings. How could the Canadian taxpayer save money when every dollar he could normally put aside is taken or confiscated so to speak, by income tax? What does such a situation lead to?
As a result, the economic and industrial development of Canada is seriously set back because Canadians simply cannot afford to save the capital required for investment.
It is all very well for the minister to travel across the country and deliver great speeches on the need for Canada to control its industry. Those are fine statements of intent but it would be much more important for the minister to give the Canadian people the financial means to save and invest those savings in Canadian productive industries. Otherwise, we will unavoidably have complete foreign control over our industry. Unfortunately, there is no other outcome for the stand taken by the minister on that matter.
That is where the minister will lead us, and this would be a result we would all deplore.
At this stage where this budget resolution respecting Income Tax Act is being discussed, I believe the Minister of Finance, who is the high priest of finance in Canada, should not try to find excuses-it is too late now that he has assumed the duties of Minister of Finance-but legislate or at least introduce in this parliament legislation to follow through or make possible the objectives which he said were his and which seemed to him so easy to reach when he sat on the opposition side.

For instance, as regards article No. 1, I wish the minister would tell us how much this provision would cost the federal treasury.
Moreover, I would like the minister to give us, if he has them at hand, the figures indicating the total number of persons to be affected by this reduction granted for tuition

That is, to my mind, giving up to a point the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) some control over education. If we look more closely at the situation, it will be realized that practically any course may be described as providing or improving the qualifications of a person for employment. Indeed, even a classical course, in the terms devoted to literature or the humanities, or similar things, may very well be put forward as helping people improve their knowledge and general training, and increase their chances of securing more remunerative and responsible employment.
Therefore, I would say that the provision should be extended not only to courses recognized by the Minister of Labour, but also to courses which could be recognized by agencies coming under the provincial departments of public education or the secretary of the province which has no department of public education; I think the provisions of section 1(d) are on the one hand too restrictive and on the other they are not restrictive enough if the Minister of Labour can decide what courses are eligible under the special provisions of that section.
No doubt the Minister of Finance will clear up the matter and assure us that the federal government has no underlying intention of interfering in a strictly provincial field.
As far as the $25 limit concerning the deduction for tuition fees is concerned, I feel

Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wanted to make concerning the Income Tax Act in general -and more particularly with regard to paragraph 1. I would be pleased if the minister would give me the proper answers as I am particularly anxious to get them.

I wonder if the minister could tell us why it is that changes are made each year in the income tax return forms? Each year they have different wording that has the same meaning, but it confuses a lot of people. Surely it is not necessary to change forms each year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member has a good point and possibly the Department of National Revenue, when it is striving for perfection, strives a little hard on occasion. The trouble is that as we change the law from year to year in parliament we complicate the lives of people who draw up these forms, as well as the lives of the people who have to pay the taxes. On behalf of the Acting Minister of National Revenue I can assure my hon. friend that his officials do the best they can. Perhaps it would be better if the form were not changed every year, and I will put the suggestion to the minister.

The forms should be in the simplest language possible, so that people may understand it. It may be all very well for people with good education; but a lot of people who have to make out these forms and pay income tax do not have much education, and the result is that they have to get the services of a chartered accountant to assist them in completing the forms.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few comments on paragraph 1 with regard to education. I think the minister has recognized that education is a very important thing in Canada today, and we have only to look at a few figures to realize how expensive it is.
Automation has made education a national necessity for our survival. Over the past three years our elementary and secondary school population have more than doubled, while our total population only increased by a little over 14 per cent. During the same period our educational expenses increased by 382 per cent. Very careful note should be taken of this, and also of the fact that during the same period of time these expenses represented an increase from 2.5 per cent to almost 5 per cent of our gross national product.

In a period of five years enrolment in universities increased from 86,000 to over 141,000, and this pace will increase more and more.
I feel that education must be national in scope. Indeed, this was recognized by the federal government when we built vocational schools, or rather when we assisted provinces to build vocational schools and paid three-quarters of the cost of building and equipping them. As a matter of fact, the previous Conservative government spent over $300 million on a crash program to train young men and women in readiness for automation. I should like to say to the minister that education imposes a very heavy burden on the municipalities. Around 50 per cent of the municipal tax dollar today goes into education and I should like to suggest to the minister that this 50 per cent should be allowed as an exemption. I think this is important because 70 per cent of the taxpayers in municipalities have incomes of $4,000 or less.
I know that part time and full time students are to be allowed exemptions if the fee is $25 or over. I am a little puzzled about paragraph 2, which reads:
That for the 1964 and subsequent taxation years a dependant in respect of whom a taxpayer may deduct an amount not exceeding $550 in computing his taxable income shall include a taxpayer's brother or sister who was 21 years of age or over and in full time attendance at a school or university.
I should like to ask the minister why this does not apply to a father or a mother of those dependants-or does it? I am not clear of the amounts. It would look as it if did not apply to a father, a mother, or even a widow-would the minister state present exemptions.
Then I should like to go on to another clause, and ask if the minister intends to allow professional people such as lawyers, dentists and doctors exemptions in respect of postgraduate courses which do not lead to a degree. I should like to ask the minister another question: What is the position of those who are taking agricultural courses, sometimes of short duration, which do not lead to a degree. Are they to be allowed the same exemption? Then I am wondering about equipment. Does this apply to a trade school and, if it does, will the students be allowed exemptions in respect of the tools and equipment it may be necessary for them to buy to take the courses. This is an important point. I am also wondering whether any provision has been made for those in the rural areas who have to travel 20 or 30 miles to take this training. Is this travelling to be allowed as an exemption? It is much harder for a fellow who has to get transportation in order to attend a night school to take his course.

Another thing I wish to comment on is the baby bonus. I want to congratulate the minister on paying this up to the ages of 16 and 17 but I am wondering why he quit before they got out of high school. If these two ages of 16 and 17 are sound, and I agree with the minister it is certainly sound to allow a boy or girl to continue his or her education for those years, it is equally sound to help them finish their course because their earning power will be much higher and they will become a much greater asset to the country. I should like the minister to explain this or reconsider it in the future so that we may carry them over high school, because it does increase their earning power and it comes back as an asset to the country.

Before making a few observations on paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of the resolution I wish to say that we seem to be getting into a more confused and complicated state of taxation all the time. Each year it is becoming more and more difficult to make out our income tax, and it has even got to the position where we have to hire auditors to do the work. I think all one can say of the amendments which the minister brought up last year and is bringing up this year is that they have provided a great deal of work for auditors throughout the country, and we shall have to hire more auditors if we are going to keep up with this. There is nothing in this resolution offering any hope of lower taxes. It is a resolution to a coat-tail budget. The United States introduced reductions in taxation. Any economic upsurge there will spill over into this country and the minister will reap some of the benefit. Therefore, he felt, it was not necessary for him to make those reductions.
Last fall he increased our income tax by 1 per cent in the old age pension section and stepped it up to a maximum of $120. So we see no reduction. We see increases. This is the situation we are confronted with. I propose to confine my remarks to paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 which have to do with changes in the regulations appertaining to the designated areas. I can only surmise that these changes were brought in because it has been a flop. I am speaking of the proposals as far as bringing industries to these areas is concerned. A question appeared on the order paper the other day asking how many industries have been attracted by the designated areas legislation brought in by the Liberal government, and we were told there were some 34. I think there were 35 areas designated in the whole of Canada, so we have less than one per designated area established under this new legislation of the Liberal government.

Income Tax Act
I should be ruled out of order, I am sure, if I were to attempt to deal with the question of designated areas. I certainly hope that at some time when the estimates of the Department of Industry come before the committee we shall be able to debate the designation of these areas. We have legislation. It was brought about under that act last fall and now we are asked in paragraph 3 to extend the benefits to industries locating in designated areas. We are asked to extend these for four years from December 5, 1963 to March 31, 1967. As I said at the beginning, this seems to be put in here to attract these industries because the former provisions were not palatable enough. So they are saying: Let us extend this for another four years and see if we cannot attract more industries into these areas. Therefore, the country as a whole is being asked to extend this for four years. I would say we would approve this in principle, but we would not approve the basis upon which these areas are designated.
So we go on to paragraph 4. In paragraph 4 the government is asking us to change section 71A of the act whereby, as I understand it-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-the machinery that is used by a company located in a designated area, under the act as it now stands, has to be 95 per cent new equipment. Now they are asking us to change the act so that this machinery shall be valued at the fair market value; in other words, they are going to make it possible to use second hand machinery. This makes it possible for an industry to move from a town into a designated area and use second hand machinery. They would be able to remove the machinery they are using, start up in one of these areas and reap the benefits of the incentives set up in the act.
I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Finance what they had to say about this matter on November 7 last. At that time there was some discussion as to the value of such machinery and whether it should be new or second hand. As reported at page 4496 of Hansard, the Minister of Industry said:
I suggest this is what is most likely to happen if the present legislation is amended so as to allow the advantages of accelerated depreciation and income tax incentives in respect of second hand or used machinery. It is precisely to avoid the likelihood of businesses which, rather than expanding and creating new operations, merely shift their scene of operation from one area to another that we need this provision.
That is why this provision was put in, as I see it, that the machinery should be 95 per cent new if you are going into one of these designated areas. Now they are asking us to put on it a fair market value. What is a fair

market value? I presume they mean that if a machine is listed in a company's books as having an actual cash value of, say $15,000, if it was sold on the market that day and brought $5,000, that would be its fair market value and they would be able to use this machinery in moving into a designated area. The Minister of Finance was down in Windsor last November and was asked a question down there concerning this matter. The gentleman asking him the question said:
Could you give me a quick clarification of the significance of "new" in this context? If I just change the name of my business but I continue to do the same as before, does this mean it is new?
Mr. Gordon replied:
No, but if you form a subsidiary and you build a great big plant next door, it is new.
That question and answer, quoted to the Minister of Finance by an hon. member, drew from the minister the answer:
With new equipment.
As I understand it, this very situation exists at the present time in the city of Galt. I am sorry the hon. member for Waterloo South is not here. As the house knows, he has been sick for some time, and I am sure we wish him a speedy recovery. In the city of Galt an industry has been operating for a few years; they are going to pack up and move over to Brantford, and as I understand it they can now take the second hand machinery they have and qualify for the incentives outlined in paragraph 4.
Paragraph 5 is just a matter of continuity. As the minister explained earlier, an area that is now in existence as a designated area, should it cease to be a designated area the plants or industries situated there can continue and reap the benefits under which they went into that area. So they are asking us, under paragraph 5, to grant continuity of the act respecting incentives for operating in designated areas.
Mr. Chairman, I think this covers what I wanted to say on these three paragraphs, 3, 4 and 5. I say again in conclusion what I said at the beginning. It would appear to me that this legislation concerning designated areas has not been successful, and so these changes are brought about in order to make it work a little better and in the hope that it might be successful. I am sorry that we cannot talk about the way in which these areas are designated, but this we will have a chance to do when the industry act is before us for consideration, or perhaps the estimates of the Department of Industry.

Mr. Chairman, I am interested in paragraph No. 2, under which in respect of a brother or sister a taxpayer is allowed to deduct an amount not exceeding $550 if

his brother or sister is a student. I would like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that $550 deductible from your income tax in respect of a student who lives in the city where the institution or university is situated, is fair and the amount is reasonable; but when a student from the country has to attend school or university in a city his expenses are much higher. These expenses have to cover board and lodging and travelling. I think those who supply the money for this education should be able to deduct at least double that amount; that is, $1,100.
Another thing that I think should be taken into consideration is this. When students have finished their college education and continue their training in hospitals as interns, their parents are not allowed any greater deduction in tax, although this internship is part of their training and involves extra expenses. It is true that some of these students are receiving a certain amount of remuneration, but this far from covers their expenses while they are interns in hospital. I think the minister should take this matter into consideration because, as I said, many students have finished their studies and have received their degrees, but they must serve a period of internship in hospital before they are granted their certificate to practise medicine. I think this is a hardship which many, many parents have to bear in regard to such tuition fees and expenses. Although, as I said before, they are granted a certain allowance which is deductible from income tax, nevertheless this is much less than the cost involved during the period of internship. I would like to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and would ask him to give it his serious consideration.
On paragraph 2, Mr. Chairman, I would just like to ask the minister whether this paragraph would include legally adopted individuals, legally adopted brothers or sisters, or children in general.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure it would include a legally adopted child, but I do not think you can legally adopt a brother.

Mr. Chairman, just one or two points on paragraph 1 before it is passed. This paragraph deals with aid to those who are taxable and are receiving higher education. I am thinking particularly of a person who is not earning a taxable income but who is still having his education paid for by his parents. I believe his parents cannot claim the cost of his tuition as an exemption. I suggest that the minister and his department give serious consideration to making such a provision in the case of parents
Income Tax Act
who are bearing the cost of their children's education, their children in turn, for one reason or another, not earning a taxable income.
In the past few years we have made great strides with the establishment of vocational schools. Efforts have been made to raise the standards of education, as well as the standards of labour generally throughout the country. I think provision should also be made in this clause for students who are going to these vocational schools to cover the cost of the tools of their trade, which are really part and parcel of their tuition. Such has long been the case for farmers and people in other professions, who can write off as a capital cost allowance the tools which help them to derive their income. While we are making provision for students to acquire tools to attend vocational school, we should also make similar provision for mechanics, who after they graduate from vocational school go out and earn their living, to write off their tools as a capital cost allowance. In a world which is fast automating and becoming highly mechanized we must be prepared to make provision for these people training in our vocational schools prior to their entry into society. We must give them an equal footing with the other professions. In some cases, such as mechanics, X-ray technicians, and so on, costly tools are required.
The minister should give, however, some thought to the suggestion that parents be allowed to write off their children's tuition fees, and also that vocational school students and mechanics should likewise be able to write off the cost of their tools as an expense incurred in the earning of their income.

I should like to ask one other question. The figures that the minister has given us are estimates of what might be spent if all of these projects are approved and the industries go ahead. As I recall it, the minister said that at the moment there are 40 which have actually been processed. In that 40 how much is involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Perhaps I might make clear that the terms "application" and "processed" really do not have too much validity. A company or firm which establishes a new enterprise in a designated area and comes into commercial operations within the required period is entitled, provided it meets certain conditions in respect of unused machinery to the value of 95 per cent and getting into operation within the required period, to the income tax incentive, and it does not depend on the approval of an application to the Department of Industry. So it is quite possible that there are a number of firms which have undertaken the establishment of new industries and have not yet informed the department. I can think of one by way of example, a very large textile operation which is being established in St. Jean, Quebec. The company had a sod turning ceremony and made an announcement of what they were going to do, and when, but prior to this taking place no information was furnished to the Department of Industry. No application was made because they do not have to apply. They merely have to enter into commercial operation, have the requisite amount of new machinery and get a certificate from the minister to this effect and they qualify.
Did that textile industry move from some area to a designated area, or was it a new industry created in that area?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: This is brand new.

I think the minister has been most vague in this respect. At least I am unable to get from his remarks the information that I think we are all desirous of obtaining. We want to know how successful the incentive program has been in the establishment of new industries in designated areas. Surely the minister must know how many of these industries have now commenced operations in these areas and have applied for the incentive benefits. I think the minister could be more precise. Surely he can tell us if there are four or five industries, where they have settled and whether they have already applied and will be receiving the benefits of the incentives. This is the information we would like to have. I realize that many industries may be writing and asking for more
Income Tax Act
particulars in the hope that they may be able to do this, but surely the minister can tell us that there are so many industries which have now established themselves in designated areas and have applied for the incentives, and will be receiving them when that time arrives.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that this program was only broached last July and became effective last November. Therefore it is perhaps a little unreasonable to assume that very many substantial industries would have established themselves in this short time. As the Minister of Finance has just indicated, some 40 companies have formally indicated that they intend to comply with the law and avail themselves of the benefits. These 40 industries in 14 of the 35 designated areas are planning capital investments in excess of $90 million and will involve in excess of 5,000 new jobs when in operation. They have not yet completed this and will not, indeed, for some time.
I realize the minister has repeated that possibly at least 40 industries have asked for information on this matter, but they have not established themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I said that 40 have formally signified their intention of establishing. They have not been asking for information. They have formally signified their intention of establishing.

In an answer last week, I think, to a written question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Peterborough the minister replied if I am correct, and I stand to be corrected, that there were 34 industries. Will the minister tell us now how many have been actually established? Has there been one, have there been four or has there been none?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I do not think that there is one that has come into commercial operations yet.
Will the minister not say that Magnetic Metals situated in Brantford is one?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I do not think Magnetic Metals is in commercial operation.

With relation to the order paper question of the hon. member for Wel-lington-Huron, which was answered by the Minister of Industry, I note that the minister sets out that in New Brunswick there are two and in Nova Scotia three of these 34 industries. As this is a high unemployment area I wonder whether the minister could now tell us the areas of Nova Scotia and the areas of New Brunswick where these five out of the 34 industries are going to be located?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I have not got that information here. I will be glad to get it and provide it tomorrow.

I should like to ask the minister if he has had any complaints from Saskatchewan that this legislation is discriminatory and is seriously handicapping the efforts of the province to diversify by bringing more industry into the province?

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I have had complaints from Saskatchewan, or for that matter from any other province.
Would the minister enlarge on paragraph 4 a little more with regard to what is meant by fair market value?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I take it we have completed discussion of paragraph 3?

Subject to being able to review these answers I think it would be perfectly agreeable to the committee to proceed, provided we can ask for further information with respect to the details as to paragraph 3 and, in fact, paragraphs 4 and 5 as well.

speechtext: I am wondering if the committee might not get into difficulty. I do not know what the intention of hon. members is and how many paragraphs will be passed tonight but perhaps we can-
