The Minister of Industry has told us he will have definite information tomorrow afternoon. I am sure hon. members of the committee would like to know the areas in which these industries have been established. I think we might make more progress if we allowed these matters to stand.
I should like the minister's comment also with regard to the effect of this incentive. I do not want to get into an argument but it has been reported in the press I believe that the Minister of Transport, speaking about the Atlantic provinces development board, stated there had been an application made by the Nova Scotia government for grants from the Atlantic provinces development board for direct capital assistance to industry. This is not the place to argue the matter, Mr. Chairman,

but I am prepared to enter into an argument at any time with the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Industry that these direct grants are much more useful than the incentives which we have before us. I hope we can allow these matters to stand and discuss them tomorrow. If the committee is prepared to move on, speaking only for the official opposition, then we are prepared to move to other items and get the information on these items tomorrow.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed?

Agreed.
Paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 stand.
On paragraph 6.

I should like to make some very general remarks on paragraph 6, Mr. Chairman. Did the Minister of Finance receive any representations relating to this paragraph in so far as it may affect or accelerate the so-called brain drain from Canada? Did bodies like the national research council make any representations relating to the paragraph and the adverse effect it might have in creating a situation whereby Canadian scientists would go to the United States? Could the minister assure us that we recognize that companies are allowed, as he explained this provision, to write off 150 per cent of the expenses relating to research done in Canada?
We are told this paragraph is going to permit a write-off for research done outside of Canada. Will this lessen the attractiveness for companies doing research in Canada? Does the minister feel this will in any way discourage Canadian companies from doing a fair amount of their research within this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This will not affect the incentive of the 150 per cent write-off in any way at all. There were a number of companies who made the complaint, not about the high level of brain drain, but the low level of taxes they would have to pay. They thought perhaps when the 150 per cent write-off provision was drafted and introduced a year or two ago, it had been drafted in such a way that people who had normal expenses in connection with research they had been carrying on outside the country for many years, and which could not be translated into Canada, were being discriminated against. They made a good case. It is recommended that they should be able to carry on as before and claim their expenses, just as they are entitled to claim any other expenses if, as it says here, they are of a nature related to scientific research which is related to the taxpayer's business.
The minister is quite certain that expenditures made outside the country were deductible prior to the amendment of 1962?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I have not checked the authorities, and I accept the statement of the minister with regard to that. My understanding was that was not the case, but possibly it was changed when we brought in the incentives, and deductions for expenditures made outside the country were disallowed. My understanding of the thing was that they were not allowed unless they were made in Canada.
As I have said before, there was a very good reason for the government giving those incentives. I know there were some who took a rather dim view of it, but the government took the responsibility for this action and I think the government was right, despite the criticism of some people who had to deal with the matter. We were faced with a situation, as the minister well knows, of a continuous drain of our experts and our professional people who were attracted to the south. It was felt at that time by giving this inducement, this incentive, industry would build up a body of technical people here in Canada, who would, otherwise, be attracted to the United States or elsewhere. How successful we were, I do not know, but certainly an effort was made in that direction.
I certainly understand the feelings of some people with regard to this matter. After I spoke about it during the budget debate, and criticized it, I received one or two letters from good friends of mine pointing out very forcibly the fact that I was being unfair in the attitude I took, and that certainly they should be allowed this deduction. I am not going to debate that too strenuously tonight. We are torn between two desires, to build up a scientific and technical organization within Canada, and at the same time be fair to corporations which have, for one reason or another, to go outside of this country to have their research work done. It is a matter of choice, and the minister has decided that the act should be amended to provide for these expenditures. He has taken us back to 1962, apparently, when this was first changed. I am not quarrelling with it, but I register a caveat because I am not quite sure if we have the technical organization here. Except in special circumstances, I think the research work should be done here. The very thing we were trying to avoid was having the research work done outside of Canada when it could be done here.
As I have said, it is a technical problem, and one which is involved. I am not going to spend more time discussing it. I am glad to see the incentive is still being kept. I think that really is worth while. I hope that Canadian corporations will continue to take 20220-168
Income Tax Act
advantage of that rather than have research work done somewhere else, in view of the fact these expenses are deductible.

The hon. member who has just spoken, Mr. Chairman, has only too well underlined the real need in Canada today to build up scientific research, to engage in scientific research within our own borders. I should like to make this remark especially, that all hon. members consider to what a great degree our manufacturing establishments in Canada are owned by parent firms across the border. If we do not insist on policing this provision very well, that this write-off can only be granted for scientific research done in Canada, I think we are going to get into serious trouble. I should like an assurance from the minister that this provision is going to be very closely policed to make sure that 100 per cent of these writeoffs will apply to research activity which obviously cannot be carried out within Canada at the present time or the foreseeable future. Otherwise, I think we would be running into serious danger of encouraging an exodus of our scientific brains to the United States, something which I think all hon. members recognize is highly undesirable.
On paragraph 6, I am not sure whether this means research by an institute for a group of individuals, or for an individual. Could it be research by an individual on behalf of himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These are expenditures which, in the main, have been made by Canadian subsidiary companies to their parent companies or to research organizations in other countries. It is mainly corporations that are concerned. In the past they were just treated as expenditures and, as I understand it, allowed as expenditures. Nobody raised a question as to what kind of expenditures they were.
Would they be subject to withholding tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt it very much. There was not a withholding tax in those days. When the amendment came in and there was particular reference to scientific research, they started to get disallowed, and understandably complained as they were in the nature of expenditures which bring pretty valuable information and know-how to Canada.

I am thinking of a medical clinic, or group of doctors working together. Could they send one doctor to university or an institute to do research, and write this off as an expense?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a clinic or group of doctors in partnership are paying one of their number, in some form or another, a salary or something like it, and they decide it is in their collective interest to send him off some place to do research, and he comes back and they get the benefit of it, I think that would be considered an expense in the earning of the income. But when you get down to this sort of question, they involve legal opinions of a very technical kind. I think this would be the case, but I hope the lawyers in the committee will not think I am moving in on their territory, because that is a very dangerous thing for an accountant to do.

Could one doctor do it-undertake research to improve himself when it is particularly related to the taxpayer's business? Could he improve himself with a postgraduate course and charge that off as research expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think that unlikely, because if he were away long enough he would not have income here to pay tax on.

That is not a good enough excuse. We will leave it to the doctor's patients to decide whether or not he has a practice to come back to. It cannot be slid off that easily. The paragraph says:
-in computing income all expenditures of a current nature...
(b) to an approved association, university, college, research institute or other similar institution to be used for scientific research related to the taxpayer's business.
This is a serious question and I do not want it sloughed off lightly by saying he will not have any patients left. I am thinking particularly of a medical man.
Or a lawyer.

Well, a medical man is what I am thinking of right now. There are many fields of research in medicine, and doctors must keep abreast of them. The minister has referred to a group of doctors who form a clinic and work as a unit, but I am asking whether a doctor can take a month's leave of absence, or two months from his practice, to do research on a given subject, such as the heart, cancer or leukemia, and write that off as a research expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are getting into a distinction between a capital expenditure and a current expenditure. This is very difficult, and I am not going to be able to give a yes or no answer. If there are a group of doctors who send one man off, and they are continuing to receive income so that there is something to deduct it from, I should think they could deduct that expenditure from their collective income. However, if one doctor does it, and
[Mr. Horner (Acadia) .1
even if he went for a couple of months and he has income to deduct it from, I would think there is a good chance the department would rule this was a capital expenditure on his part. I cannot give a definitive answer on that. Perhaps we could call on the ex-minister of national revenue, who held that position for many years, and possibly his opinion would be as good as any.

We are dealing with a general resolution here. There will be a bill before us shortly, an income tax bill, in which the details will be spelled out, and I would suggest at that time that the minister be prepared to answer these questions so far as he can, bearing in mind the fact that the Department of National Revenue always takes a very dim view of anybody making a ruling in advance. My colleague from Queens-Lunen-burg wants to know if he sends a trawler out scouting for new fishing grounds, and if that can be described as scientific research, could he deduct that expense? The hon. member for Acadia and others will have many more questions to ask when the bill is before us, and I suggest that the minister be prepared to deal with their questions then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member has demonstrated very well how he was such a success as minister of national revenue.

When the bill comes before us I hope there will be something in it to indicate that a company, let us say company X, controlled in the United States and doing business in Canada, and which is now carrying on research activities in Canada, will not transfer those activities to the United States just to take advantage of this provision, particularly when these research activities can be undertaken in Canada.
The minister was quite right in saying this law is the same as it was before. I shall certainly take his word for that, but I believe it is immaterial because today we are faced with the problem of keeping our scientific research institutions and our better scientific brains in Canada. I would like to see some indication that the advantage which is being given will not make it attractive to carry on research activities in the United States which can now be carried on in Canada.
However, where it is patently obvious that a research activity is of such a scale that it could only be carried on in the United States, then there should be such a beneficial clause. Without taking any more time of the committee I would like to point out what could be a very serious problem in closing this gap, and I hope it will not make it too attractive for companies to move research establishments over the border.

I think the government is asking us to pass a resolution here that we will regret the day we pass it. As I understand it, a United States subsidiary operating in Canada and doing research work here in Canada would now have a great temptation to cease that research and do it in the parent office in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I try to explain that, and also to answer the question put by the hon. member tor Brome-Missisquoi. Under the law at present, any Canadian company has a great incentive to do its research work in Canada. If it does its research work in Canada it is allowed to charge off against its income for tax purposes 150 per cent of the expense of research-not just 100 per cent, but 150 per cent; that is, 150 per cent of the increase. If it continues to do what has been done over the years-pay someone in the United States or in Britain or in some other country for access to the kind of research it could not get anywhere else; I cannot imagine that it would be making the payments otherwise-then over the years it has been allowed to deduct those expenditures for tax purposes. This stopped in 1962 because of the wording of the amendment at that time and the way in which it was interpreted by the tax officers.
The purpose of this amendment is to put things back where they were prior to 1962, as far as the regular, historical, traditional expenditures for technical services and so on are concerned. We did not change in any way the special incentive which was introduced in 1962 to encourage people to do more research in Canada. The incentive is there. It is merely being suggested that the penalty should be removed.
Paragraph 6 agreed to.
On paragraph 7.

Paragraph 7, I think in the terms in which it is couched, is an amazing disposition. I think probably as a lawyer I should not attack this provision at all because if ever I move out of this place and go back into practice I may be able to make a few dollars out of it.
You won't need to, with your majority.

That is a wise observation. If I was not afraid of being ruled out of order I would say I have excellent prospects of at least doubling my majority.
In any event this is the provision which is of interest to a number of us around here and I think the minister should give us some details of the manner in which it will operate. Of course, the gist of it is that if a taxpayer 20220-1684
Income Tax Act
appeals an assessment he may in the following taxation year, I imagine, deduct any expenditures that he has incurred either in filing the opposition or in registering an appeal from an assessment. But what comes to my mind is this: Does the minister intend to put a ceiling on the amount of expenditure which may be incurred in filing an opposition or making an appeal.
Seeing the provision of this section, if a taxpayer is in a position where he must file an appeal or oppose an assessment, because of the very generous disposition of the minister he will engage the best legal lights in the country to take up his case. That is understandable. But as the minister, no doubt, knows, not all lawyers charge the same fees. The services of some are expensive and in other cases their services are more expensive; so it can be expected that the taxpayer might resort to the best legal talent and therefore the highest fees of the land. They might run into thousands of dollars. In such a case will the department foot the taxpayer's bill? If so, I think the lawyers are going to have a field day. Will these costs that are being allowed be on a client-solicitor basis or will they be costs to be taxed according to a tariff?
I think this paragraph is lacking in the way it is drafted, because there is no mention at all as to the nature of the costs that may be deductible or whether a tariff will be established or not-if a bill of costs will be submitted to a taxation authority or if taxation by the board of appeal clerk, or some officer in the board of appeal, will be conclusive evidence of the real cost incurred by the taxpayer and, if so, whether the Minister of National Revenue will have any discretion at all in allowing or disallowing the claim for deductions because of legal costs to fight an assessment.
Another thought that comes to my mind is that this provision will certainly give rise in my opinion to a considerable interest in the number of formal oppositions and appeals, and this may throw an extra burden on the board of appeals. I think this is a good moment to think of the functions which that board fulfils and to renew a request which has been made by others on this side of the house on various occasions to make this board a fully fledged court, with permanency of tenure and so on. If you are going to give to that board the responsibility that it exercises at present and also the added burden with which it will be faced, the government might well consider the feasibility of converting the board into a court. That, I think, would also result perhaps in a better administration of this board and in better results from the important functions it is performing.

Income Tax Act
Another question I should like to ask in regard to this paragraph is whether or not the minister envisages the payment of the cost of filing an appeal from the formal opposition. Does it include legal costs which may have been incurred by the taxpayer for advice as to whether or not an appeal should be undertaken, and does it also include costs that may be incurred after the judgment, for instance, with regard to services rendered in connection with making arrangements for the service of a debt for tax? Will it also apply to expenses incurred by the taxpayer at higher levels, in the exchequer court and the supreme court? This is new law and as such it certainly opens a door to a large number of questions and possibilities and maybe even loopholes. This present paragraph is very incomplete and, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said a few minutes ago in regard to paragraph 6, we will be anticipating the bill with a great deal of interest; and also, I imagine, the amendments to the Income Tax Act that are foreseen by paragraph 7 will be looked at very closely to ascertain just how far the minister intends to go with this new and rather revolutionary policy that he is introducing at this time.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister replies I would like to support what the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue has said. I cannot for the life of me understand this paragraph, because we are not only dealing with appeals, as the hon. member said, on which possibly there is a tariff. There is, certainly, when you get to the exchequer court. I am not sure whether there is a tariff before the income tax appeal board; I do not think there is, but there could be. But when it comes to filing an objection, without becoming overemphatic I can say that one files an objection almost every time from any assessment. Sometimes it is simply a matter of scribbling out a letter of some kind; sometimes it is a very involved objection. There is no tariff, there is no provision in the act, as I understand, to provide for this.
Far be it from me to prevent lawyers or accountants earning by the sweat of their brow, as they always have, their fees. They are underpaid all the time, of course, as both the minister and I would agree with respect to both professions; but I cannot for the life of me see how you are going to provide for reductions for the filing of objections. The assessment may be for $1 million and you may come from Wolfville, Vancouver or Toronto, as I am sure the minister did in the days when he was practicing, and go into the office of the deputy minister and discuss the matter. There is all this matter of solicitor and client, or you may have an objection to 
a farmer's income tax, or anybody else's income tax, as far as that is concerned, for $100, $500 or whatever it may be.
On what basis are you going to be able to charge for filing this objection? I will tell the minister what in my opinion this is going to do. Every lawyer in the country and every chartered accountant who happens to have a spare five minutes on his hands is going to sit down and draft a notice of objection, and the income tax appeal board-which is swamped now by appeals; at least, it was; there were appointments made and they may be more up to date, but I am quite sure they are not caught up-will have to deal with these objections. This is going to encourage the filing of appeals, and I am sure that if the minister by any chance happened to be attending a reception one night-I will not say a cocktail party, because that language is hardly acceptable in the House of Commons -or one of these gatherings, say an embassy function somewhere, at which members of the income tax appeal board happened to be gathered, if he could hear their language with respect to what this paragraph might do -this is only guesswork on my part, you will understand, Mr. Chairman-and their opinion as to what they think this paragraph might do in increasing the appeal load, he might have different views on this subject. I do not know whether this has been recommended by the barristers association or by a joint committee of chartered accountants and lawyers-if it is, it is remarkably well sponsored-but I would suggest to the minister that he should take a very, very careful look at this paragraph. Certainly when the act is brought down it will have to be dealt with very, very carefully.

Mr. Chairman, just before the minister answers that question, perhaps he would also take note of the last part of this paragraph:
-shall Include in computing income any costs recovered in respect thereof.
It seems to me that by adding that provision they are robbing Peter to pay Paul, or vice versa, because on the one hand they say the costs are deductible and on the other hand they say that if costs are recovered they must be added to income. That leaves the taxpayer right in the middle, and nothing is given.
Another point I should like to raise is that with regard to any costs recovered, generally the costs are taxable, not in regard to the client or the party involved in the litigation, but they are taxable costs that go directly to the lawyer who has been employed in the

case, and that is an attorney of record. Therefore I cannot see how it can be that the taxpayer can recover costs on his own. Perhaps the minister would elucidate that particular point, together with the others that were raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in his first statement on this point the hon. member for Pon-tiac-Temiscamingue seemed to be fearful that as a result of this provision various clients, not of his, would transfer all their work to what he called-I do not remember the expression, but the first class lawyers.
Legal lights.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Legal lights, yes. I would not be so brave as to suggest that there was such a thing as a second class lawyer.
Sometimes our light is hidden under a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite confident that if the hon. member does not double his vote in the next election, he will find he has plenty of business of this type. I would remind him that section 12(2) of the act provides:
In computing income, no deduction shall be made in respect of an outlay or expense otherwise deductible except to the extent that the outlay or expense was reasonable in the circumstances.
If any professional man should charge a fee that was unreasonable-and I would hope this would not happen-then it would remain with the Department of National Revenue to disallow it.
Who is going to act as taxing master?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In practice, as I suspect hon. members know, the real check on anybody charging too much is the company or the client. I cannot believe that any reasonable client would allow his tax consultant to charge him twice as much as he should because he only has to pay half of it. But this was a submission made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and I believe others, over a period of years. I do not feel very strongly about it; I am not in professional practice. I think it is something, though, that is reasonable; and we should remember that whoever receives these fees will have to pay tax on them, so as far as the crown is concerned it is about six of one and half a dozen of the other.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REGULATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WHARVES BY FISHERMEN
speechtext: The first question is from the hon. member for Skeena regarding regulations respecting government wharves.

subtopic: REGULATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WHARVES BY FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my concern with these particular regulations, which are promulgated under the Government Harbours and Piers Act, is the manner in which charges are levied and their effect on fishermen. I refer in particular to the different effect of those regulations on fishermen on the east coast of Canada as compared with fishermen on the west coast. What I hope to accomplish is to pose to the minister the thought that they apply inequitably; that charges will be levied against fishermen on the west coast for the use of wharves and floats which will not be levied against fishermen on the east coast.
The reason for this is both with respect to the wording of the regulations themselves
2640	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and also with respect to the past attitude of the Department of Public Works in providing facilities for fishermen. The regulations prior to their change in January of this year used to read as follows. Rather than quote the regulations I should like to quote an extract from a copy of a letter written by Mr. J. H. W. Cavey, who is chief of the harbours and property division, to a Mr. G. W. Nickerson of the city of Prince Rupert. In his letter there is this quotation:
"No side wharfage is payable in respect to (a) Canadian fishing vessels during the first 48 hours at any wharf, (b) Canadian fishing vessels at any time at wharves other than those specified by the minister".
That is the end of the quotation from the regulations.
Then Mr. Cavey indicates the effect of these regulations was as follows:
Under these regulations fishing vessels were exempted at practically all public wharves and floats.
Then the amended regulations came into effect. I do not intend to read in any detail from a press release which I have before me, except to say that one of the reasons for bringing the new changes into effect was aimed at improving the regulations and providing for more efficient wharf administration. The fact of the matter is that under the new regulations as well as under the old-particularly now because charges will be levied for the use of wharves-the Department of Public Works has not provided what we call floats on the east coast but they have on the west coast. As a consequence charges for side wharfage will not be applied to fishermen on the east coast, because they only use wharves on the east coast for the purpose of unloading fish or for loading supplies. Fishermen on the west coast do that as well, but in addition floats have been built at which the fishermen tie up.
Usually because of the insistence of the Department of Fisheries with regard to the curtailment of the fishing week, fishermen find themselves tied up at floats for periods of two, three or four days a week. Perhaps in this coming fishing season it will be for as long as five days a week that fishermen will have to tie up at floats, rather than be out fishing for salmon, owing to the stringent restrictions imposed by the Department of Fisheries. As a consequence fishermen on the west coast will have to pay under the regulations side wharfage rates for the use of the floats, whereas the fishermen on the east coast will not. This, of course, raises the hackles of any bona fide fisherman or even the fisherman who fishes one or two days a week, because it does smack of discrimination of a sort. Fishermen are going to have a


difficult enough time on the west coast without having to pay charges for the use of floats.
In the second instance, while the press release stated that the regulations were to provide for more efficient wharf administration I submit they will not, because in the city of Prince Rupert there is a plan under way for the federal government to lease the float facilities to somebody else. In all likelihood this will be the city of Prince Rupert which will operate the floats. All that will happen will be that the city of Prince Rupert will be charging fishermen for the use of these floats and will be spending the money in two ways, first to pay the fee to the federal government under the lease agreement and, second, to employ up to eight watchmen who will in fact be toll collectors. Nothing will be accomplished in the way of providing any additional services to the fishermen or in providing efficient wharf administration, as the press release accompanying the regulations stated would be the case.
There are so many implications involved in this action and objections to it that time does not permit me to go into them in great detail, but I would point out one simple thing to the minister. At many of these floats boats tie up one beside the other, three or four or maybe five deep. Let us say for the sake of argument that some Friday night the watchman or toll collector comes down to these floats. If that watchman expects to extract the same side wharfage fee from the fishermen who ties up alongside the float as from the fisherman who has to tie up fourth or fifth boat out, he has got another think coming; and in the process of collecting the fees he may very well wind up in the water. The fishermen at home are disturbed and upset about this system.
Second, do the regulations mean that if a fisherman pays side wharfage fees for, say, a period of a month he is then permitted to tie up his boat to any float anywhere in British Columbia? I notice you are rising, Mr. Speaker, so my time must be nearing an end. I appreciate the opportunity of placing this very important matter before the house and the minister and I say sincerely to the minister: Will you please amend the regulations and put them back the way they were prior to the change in January of this year? The fishermen will be happy and they will have more money in their pockets.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REGULATIONS RESPECTING USE OF WHARVES BY FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I should start out by saying that while I can understand the feeling of a fisherman or indeed of anyone else who did not have to pay a service charge before and is asked to pay

one, there is in fact no discrimination whatsoever in the regulations, and 1 think the hon. member himself indicated that. They apply absolutely equally on the east coast and on the west coast. The appearance of discrimination is because of the entirely different conditions, which I think the hon. member outlined pretty fairly.
I must say I do not have any great familiarity with these floats on the west coast.
I have never examined them. However, it is quite true that either on the east coast or the west coast there are no side wharfage charges for commercial fishermen provided they are simply unloading or loading their vessels, and are not tied up for more than a certain length of time. On the east coast there are no floats provided at all, to the best of my knowledge, for fishermen to park their boats, if one may put it that way, or to tie them up, whereas on the west coast apparently the taxpayers have provided very considerable facilities which have been used partly by commercial fishermen.
Information has been given to me which is perhaps not as true of Prince Rupert as it may be of some other places on the west coast, and this may perhaps be the reason why it is that the main complaint so far has come from Prince Rupert.
I am told that many of these floats are used by sports fishermen or by the owners of pleasure craft. I do not believe there would be many hon. members who would argue that taxpayers should be expected to provide wharfage for that kind of vessel at public expense. If these wharves had been used exclusively by commercial fishermen, I am quite sure there would have been no thought whatever that it would not have been worth while.
I cannot go into much detail on this matter because I only have three minutes. I cannot go into much detail for another reason, namely that these regulations were made at a time when I was not the minister, nor was I here to discuss them. However, I shall look into them.

Mr. Speaker, I asked the question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to the situation in Viet Nam because there is great concern over the possibility of very early and dangerous developments there which may involve us and others as well. There has been a proposal by the United States to increase its forces and to increase
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion its direct participation in what Senator Morse has described as an illegal and unwise war. Some years ago we were told the United States had observers there. Then, they had advisers, but here we have a senator of the United States admitting that this is a war.
The second reason we are concerned at the invitation on the part of the United States to other countries to participate in these forces outside the United Nations, is that we take the strongest objection to this unilateral action on the part of the United States or any other countries associated with them. Then again, we were most dissatisfied with the brief, uninforming and unsatisfactory answer given to a question asked by our leader a day or so ago by the Prime Minister with regard to this problem. He said, in brief, that no request had been made. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a serious situation like this developing in that part of the world would warrant the Prime Minister of this country at least giving the house some statement as to the government's policy or attitude toward this unfortunate development. We believe that the government should make a clear and definite statement of policy with regard to its attitude toward the Viet Nam situation and recent developments.
This is a very serious question which has a great potential for danger to the rest of the world and should be referred to the United Nations. We most definitely oppose this unilateral action by the United States and other countries, as suggested. We believe that this situation should be handled as a result of a reference to the United Nations for a peace keeping force under the United Nations, under the rule of law that we are doing so much to try and develop in the world today. I hope the parliamentary secretary will deal with this question and leave us more satisfied with his answer than we were with the Prime Minister's answer to our leader a day or so ago.

I think the housewives of Canada would like to know from the minister whether he is prepared to do something and what he is prepared to do. They want to know if he will continue to do what he has done for the last 12 months namely, nothing, or whether he has at last formulated some policy to deal with this problem.
